original: Matrix Multiplication Matrix multiplication follows a slightly more verbose methodology than simple addition or subtraction. When multiplying matrices, each row of the previous matrix multiplies with each column of the next matrix. This will become clearer in the example to follow. One way to think of this process is that each row of the first matrix processes each column of the second matrix. Let’s firstly present two 2 x 2 matrices to multiply: To calculate the final matrix (that is currently empty) each row of the first matrix needs to multiply with every column of the second matrix. The resulting matrix is known as the dot product of the matrices being multiplied. Dot products are widely used in machine learning, with NumPy supplying their own dot function to leverage. This process is admittedly is extremely hard to visualise, so let’s break it down into stages. The first row and column process resembles the following: Notice that we’re starting with the first row of matrix 1, and the first column of matrix 2. The corresponding values are multiplied, with their products added together resulting in one dot product value. Since there are more columns to multiply, row 1 then multiples with the next column of matrix 2: Now row 1 of matrix 1 has processed all columns of matrix 2, we can repeat the whole process for row 2: And finally process the last column of matrix 2 with the currently active row of matrix 1: And this concludes the dot product process. We can now simplify the resulting matrix with its true values: This concludes the dot product process! However, there are some requirements in order for a multiplication to be valid. The above example multiplies two matrices of shape 2 x 2 for simplicity, but there are a couple of rules that one must be aware of when dealing with matrix multiplication that pertains to the shapes and ordering of the matrices being multiplied. Let’s briefly take a look at these requirements. The requirements of matrix multiplication Even though the size of the matrices being multiplied does not need to be the same, the inner numbers must match. This requirement is obviously always met in the case of square matrices, but when the dimensions are different, then the column count of matrix 1 must match the row count of matrix 2. The shape of the resulting matrix is also determined by the shapes of the multiplying matrices— their outer numbers to be exact. These two rules are summarised in the following multiplication: Outer values determine the resulting shape, and the inner values must be the same for the multiplication to be valid, or defined. If the inner values are not the same, the resulting matrix will be undefined. Because of these requirements, it is not possible to multiply a non-square matrix with itself! The result would be undefined. This would entail multiplying, for example, a 2 x 3 matrix with a 2 x 3 matrix, and the inner numbers here do not match. We could however do an element-wise multiplication, that will be mentioned further down. With multiplication, ordering also matters Unlike scaler products, the resulting matrix will differ depending on which way round the matrices are in your formula. In other words, matrix multiplication is not commutative. If we take the product of two regular numbers, it does not matter which way round they are multiplied. E.g: 6 x 4 = 24 A x B 4 x 6 = 24 B x A == Same result This is not the case with matrices. Re-ordering even the simplest of matrices yields a drastically different dot product: Dot product vs element-wise multiplication Another type of matrix multiplication is known as element-wise multiplication. This is where each index of matrix A is multiplied with matrix B.
sampled: Michelle Jaqua had been trying to lose 20 lbs for 2 years before she finally turned to Whole30, a diet program that strips away nearly every comfort food category in one go. The program eliminates sugar, carbs, alcohol, dairy, legumes, corn, peanuts, and preservatives, leaving a very narrow path through the grocery store. The first two weeks demanded a complete overhaul of how Michelle cooked and thought about meals, pushing her toward ingredients she had rarely centered a plate around before. Her daily staples settled into eggs, ghee butter, spinach, yams, and coconut-based foods, a rotation that was simple but required consistent preparation. Because so many packaged sauces and condiments contain sugar or preservatives, Michelle began making nearly everything from scratch in her own kitchen. She produced homemade mayo, dressings, sauces, a coconut curry sauce, chicken broth, and a cabbage and meat soup that became a reliable option throughout the month. Swapping familiar carbohydrate-heavy dishes also became part of the routine, and one substitution that worked well was using spaghetti squash in place of regular spaghetti. The texture is different enough that it requires a mental adjustment, but it allowed her to keep a satisfying dinner format without breaking the program's rules. By day 13, the effort was producing measurable results, and Michelle had lost 5 lbs while also reporting better sleep, more energy, and fewer migraines than she had been experiencing before the diet. Those physical changes arrived together rather than one at a time, which made the restrictive food list feel more worthwhile. Day 14 brought a more personal milestone when Michelle went wedding dress shopping and found that she fit into a lower clothing size after losing those five pounds. She said "Yes" to the wedding dress that day, a moment made possible in part by the physical change she had already achieved in just two weeks on the program. Not every day went smoothly, and day 17 introduced a complication when Michelle came down with a head cold and took cold medicine even though it technically fell outside Whole30 rules. That small deviation was a practical concession rather than an abandonment of the program, and she continued following the diet through the remainder of the month. By day 25, Michelle had lost 9 lbs, and the change in her body was significant enough that she spent $500 on new clothes to fit her smaller frame. She found one pant style that worked well enough that she bought it in 3 colors, a practical response to the reality that her previous wardrobe no longer fit correctly. The final stretch of the 30 days held steady, and by day 30 Michelle had officially lost 10 pounds and dropped a full clothing size from where she had started. The 2 years of unsuccessful attempts to lose 20 lbs made that 10-pound result feel concrete and earned rather than accidental. Beyond the number on the scale, the physical changes that had begun showing up early in the program continued through the end of Whole30. Michelle reported better sleep and decreased migraines by the time she completed the full 30 days, benefits that had nothing to do with clothing size or weight. The cooking habits she built during the month, making sauces, broths, and soups from scratch and relying on whole ingredients like eggs, ghee, and yams, had become familiar enough that continuing them did not feel like a burden. That familiarity made the idea of keeping the eating style in place after the program ended a realistic option rather than a distant aspiration. After completing Whole30, Michelle considered adopting the eating style as a permanent lifestyle rather than returning to the habits that had kept her stuck for 2 years. The combination of weight loss, better sleep, fewer migraines, and a wardrobe that finally fit gave her a set of specific, concrete reasons to keep going.

original: Equity crowdsale: what’s next? Here’s a breakdown of next steps and what to expect. In case you missed the big news from the weekend: the BABB equity crowdsale closed at 11:59pm on Saturday 18 August, with total investment coming in at just over £1,550,000 from 1,452 investors. We’re delighted to have been successfully funded and are very grateful to all of our new shareholders for their support. What’s next? There is a lot happening over the next few weeks. Here’s everything you need to know if you invested in the equity crowdsale. Follow-up info There now follows a seven-day period in which Crowdcube will send out additional information, including articles of association. This is an official document which outlines BABB’s responsibilities as a business to you as a shareholder. Please read it carefully and get in touch if you have any questions. Confirming your ID Crowdcube might also contact you to submit ID for KYC and AML checks. In most cases they perform these checks automatically but some investors will need to supply additional documentation. If you’re in any doubt about whether you need to submit any documentation, we advise logging into your Crowdcube account or contacting the customer support team. We’re also on hand to help if you need us; you can chat to the team in the dedicated equity crowdsale telegram group or email us at crowdsale@getbabb.com. Making the payment If you pledged via credit or debit card, your investment will be taken automatically early next week. If you pledged to invest via bank transfer, Crowdcube will contact you about arranging the payment. You can also refer to our previous blog post for further instructions. Receiving your shares Once you have passed KYC and made your investment, your shares will be automatically distributed to your Crowdcube account within 2–3 weeks. You will be able to view and manage your portfolio through your account on the Crowdcube website. You will also receive an official share certificate confirming you as a shareholder in BABB Group Ltd. Please enjoy it and keep it safe! BAX bonus and airdrop Once Crowdcube has confirmed payment from all investors, we will receive email addresses for all participants. We will then be able to get in touch directly regarding claiming the BAX bonus and airdrop. If you already have an account on getbabb.com (from the token sale), you will automatically receive your BAX bonus and airdrop into this account. Please note that if the email address linked to your Crowdcube account is different to the one linked to your BABB account, you will need to let us know. If you don’t have a BABB account, we will contact you directly with instructions to open an account on getbabb.com. You will need to open this account in order to claim the BAX bonus and airdrop. The BAX bonus is payable to all equity crowdsale investors and is dependent on the amount invested. The BAX airdrop is distributed to all those who participated in the BABB token sale as as well as all those who invested in the equity crowdsale. All recipients will recieve the same number of tokens in the airdrop and we’ll contact you nearer the time to confirm the airdrop amount. Sharehodler merch competition We recently selected the winners of our sharehodler merch competition and everyone who took part in the competition has received an email letting them know whether or not they were among the winners. The last of the merch orders is due to arrive this week (following a delay; thanks for bearing with us) so we’ll distribute the prizes to the winners as soon as we can. Perks and rewards Speaking of merch — we will also contact investors in the coming weeks about claiming the perks they’re eligible for as a result of their invested amount.
sampled: Linda Caroll writes on Medium, and over the course of building a daily writing habit she tracked her progress carefully enough to know she missed only 2 days out of the last 20, a record that reflects genuine commitment rather than casual intention. That kind of consistency is harder to sustain than it sounds, and the fact that she kept going even imperfectly points to something more deliberate than motivation alone driving her practice. What drove her was a seven-step formula she developed specifically to write faster and with less rambling, a structural approach born from real frustration with how writing sessions can collapse into circular thinking and wasted time. The formula did not emerge from theory but from the practical need to sit down and produce something coherent without spending the session fighting her own mind. The first obstacle she names is the blank page itself, and her solution is to use constraints, such as writing prompts, to sidestep the paralysis that comes from total open-endedness. Once a topic is chosen, a second obstacle takes over, which she identifies as brain pong and rambling, the tendency for a writer's attention to bounce between half-formed ideas rather than moving the piece forward in a purposeful direction. Her formula addresses this by giving each stage of the writing process a distinct job, beginning with the topic and then moving immediately into the search for relevant data or statistics in step 2. Rather than generalizing from personal impression, the formula asks the writer to find a real source and cite it, which grounds the piece in something concrete and prevents the vague claims that make writing feel thin and untrustworthy to readers. Step 3 brings in personal experience to strengthen the story, layering a human dimension onto the factual foundation laid by the data, so that the piece carries both credibility and emotional texture at the same time. These two elements together, the cited fact and the lived moment, give the writing a kind of double footing that keeps it from tipping into either dry reporting or shapeless memoir. Only after the topic, data, and personal story are gathered does step 4 ask the writer to craft a strong opening, a sequence that runs counter to the instinct many writers have to begin at the beginning before knowing what the piece actually contains. Waiting to write the opening until the material is assembled means the opening can do real work instead of functioning as a placeholder that will need to be rewritten anyway. Step 5 connects the ending back to the beginning of the piece, creating a loop that gives readers a sense of arrival rather than simply stopping, and step 6 asks the writer to identify the emotion the piece should evoke before selecting a cover image that matches it. These steps treat the emotional and visual dimensions of the work as deliberate choices rather than afterthoughts, which changes the nature of the decisions being made about both image and tone. Step 7 is to write the title last, after re-reading the completed piece, so that the title can accurately reflect what the work turned out to be rather than what the writer hoped it might become at the start. Ideas that do not fit the current piece are not discarded but jotted down in an idea bin for later use, which keeps the session focused without losing material that might serve a future piece. Since building the formula into her practice, Linda Caroll notes that poetry keeps appearing when she opens the page to write, a detail that suggests the structure loosened something rather than tightening it. The seven steps function less like a cage and more like a cleared path, one that makes room for unexpected writing to arrive precisely because the mechanical decisions have already been handled in advance.

original: Businesses everywhere are experimenting with ways to tackle the obstacles imposed by the pandemic. For most, this is a process of trial and error. They either apply existing solutions that they are personally familiar with or copy as best they can what others around them are doing. But in some instances, like ETEN’s repurposing of micro-greenhouses, experimentation leads to genuinely novel solutions that reimagine products and services in new and exciting ways. So how do we go from deploying existing solutions to generating inspiring new approaches? It starts with how we think about resolving challenges: do we try to reconstruct the preexisting experience (even if they are at best Frankenstein-esque recreations), or pioneer new paths to discover new possibilities? Reconstruct: restoring the status-quo, or some version of it Much of our day-to-day actions unfold without much thought. We repeat routines and behaviors, allowing our experiences to guide us. The more ingrained and institutionalized they are, the less we think about them. For instance, before the pandemic, eating close to others was the norm, never crossing anyone’s mind as a serious threat to public health. As creatures of habit, we go through life like this until one of our habits or routines stops working as anticipated. When this happens, the particular stream of action we are in hits a roadblock, bringing the conflicted situation to our conscious awareness. With our automatic responses impaired by the roadblock, we consciously evaluate what other options in our repertoire of personal or socially observed experiences might help us restore the situation so that we can carry on. In most instances, quickly deploying a readily available alternative is sufficient to restore the situation. We saw this happening all across the country after states and municipalities imposed social distancing measures. The overnight introduction of takeout and make-at-home kits by elite restaurants in New York City, like Masa and Rezdôra, are prime examples. Neither strategy was part of their standard playbook, however without the ability to host guests and exorbitant overhead costs pilling up, they had to explore new ways to generate revenues. While takeout is novel to elite three-star New York Times reviewed restaurants, it is standard practice for most. This provided an immediate and easily deployable solution that, apart from the price-point, was familiar to their customers. Rezdôra’s make-at-home meal kit instructions Ultimately, Rezdôra, Masa, and, most recently, Eleven Madison Park, are trying, as best they can, to continue serving their customers within the parameters of government restrictions. All with the hope of weathering the storm and returning to their pre-pandemic operations and interactions with their guests. Omakase, after all, is an intimate and evolving interaction between you and the sushi master. If they cannot react to your every expression, playing to your likes and curiosities, the experience falls flat. Sushi masters at Sushi Gen in Los Angeles’s Little Tokyo Reimagine: pioneering a new path to new possibilities Ruptures in established routines and behaviors offer unique opportunities to reimagine how we think about and do things. During stable times, the social structures we are enmeshed in sustain and reinforce our routines and behaviors. We have all experienced the power of peer pressure. When we try to deviate from the norm, the group’s force pulls us back in line. (These same dynamics are at play at the organizational level, constraining how businesses think, act, and look.) When ruptures are systemic, throwing everyone into disarray, the power of conformity briefly loosens its grips. During these moments, we have the unique opportunity to construct new routines and behaviors, with the potential that they will catch on and become the new norm. So, how do we start pioneering new paths and possibilities? Especially given that how we see the world around us is hemmed in by our past experiences, social contexts, and technical constraints — all exerting forces that narrow our field of vision? Expanding our field of vision begins by replacing our current lenses with ones that provide new ways of seeing what we are tackling. Stripping down products and services to their core fundamentals is an effective way to gain new perspectives. Focusing on the fundamental characteristics of what we are exploring exposes the taken-for-granted assumptions and expectations that we have come to accept unconsciously. Through this awareness, we can ask how we can approach these core characteristics in new ways that better meet consumers’ evolving needs, wants, and desires.
sampled: The Los Angeles Dodgers won their first World Series since 1988, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in a season already defined by disruption and compromise. That victory celebration became the center of a serious controversy when third baseman Justin Turner returned to the field after testing positive for COVID-19. Turner had been removed from the game in the 7th inning after receiving a positive test result, but he did not stay away from his teammates once the final out was recorded by pitcher Julio Urias. He returned to the field, hugged teammates, and held the World Series trophy despite the confirmed positive test result. What made the situation more troubling was the timeline surrounding the test itself. The league had received an inconclusive result as early as the 2nd inning, yet Turner remained in the game for five more innings before being removed. Turner also removed his mask for a group photo while standing in close proximity to teammates during the on-field celebration. Reporters, photographers, and players' families were all present on the field during that same period, extending the potential exposure well beyond the roster. Reports indicated that Dodgers management may have permitted Turner to be on the field for the team photo, raising questions about whether the breach was purely an individual decision or something that involved organizational awareness. The gap between when the inconclusive result arrived and when Turner exited added weight to those concerns. MLB Commissioner Rob Manfred faced scrutiny not only for the Turner situation but for decisions made earlier in the season. In late July, the Miami Marlins reported 3 positive COVID-19 cases among their players, yet Manfred allowed the team to proceed with a scheduled game against the Philadelphia Phillies. Within days of that game, the number of positive cases on the Marlins roster had risen to 20. Manfred cited temperature checks as his justification for permitting the Marlins to play, a rationale that drew considerable criticism given how quickly the outbreak expanded. Manfred had spoken about the season's COVID-19 protocols on The Daily podcast in the context of Juan Soto testing positive ahead of the season opener. His framing was notably candid: "we knew we were going to have positives . . . The whole point is you have a system that's flexible enough to deal with what's coming. We knew it was coming." That statement, when placed alongside the Marlins decision and the Turner incident, highlighted a tension between the league's stated awareness of risk and its actual enforcement of the protocols designed to manage that risk. Flexibility, in practice, appeared to mean allowing games to proceed even when the safety calculus was uncertain. The human cost of COVID-19 exposure within the sport was real and documented throughout the season. Eduardo Rodriguez, a pitcher for the Red Sox, was unable to play at all in 2020 after developing myocarditis as a complication of his COVID-19 infection. Freddie Freeman, the Braves first baseman, suffered a 104-degree fever during his illness and reported praying for his life at the height of it. Those cases gave concrete weight to what was at stake each time protocols were treated as negotiable rather than binding. ESPN reporter Stephen A. Smith commented publicly on Turner's situation, reflecting the broader media attention the incident drew. The breach was not a quiet procedural lapse but a visible, photographed event that unfolded in front of cameras during one of the sport's highest-profile moments. The contrast between the Dodgers' historic win and the circumstances surrounding Turner's return made it difficult to separate celebration from accountability. A championship that ended a 32-year drought for the franchise was immediately shadowed by questions about what the league's protocols actually meant when tested under pressure. The Marlins outbreak and the Turner incident together illustrated a pattern in which the league's response to positive tests was inconsistent and, at times, appeared to prioritize scheduling and competition over the health of players and staff. Both situations involved known positive results and decisions that allowed continued exposure. What the 2020 season demonstrated, through the Marlins outbreak, the illnesses of players like Freeman and Rodriguez, and the World Series celebration breach, was that the gap between written protocol and enforced protocol carried genuine consequences for the people inside the sport. The Turner incident did not occur in isolation but at the end of a season full of similar decisions made at the institutional level.

original: Netlify’s platform team is responsible for building and scaling the systems designed to keep Netlify, and the hundreds of thousands of sites that use it, up and running. We take that responsibility seriously, so we’re constantly looking for potential points of failure in our system and working to remove them. Most of our platform is cloud agnostic, and since we favor an approach that minimizes risk, we wanted to extend that to include our origin services. This led to a project that culminated in us migrating our origin services between cloud providers on a recent Sunday night — without any service interruptions. When you deploy a website to Netlify, your content automatically gets pushed to the edge nodes in our Content Delivery Network (CDN). If you make changes in your Git repository, your content is continuously and automatically synced with our origin servers and pushed to the CDN. Our CDN runs on six different cloud providers, but up until recently, our origin servers relied on only one. That meant our origin servers were subject to the performance and uptime characteristics of a single provider. We wanted to make sure that in the face of a major outage from an underlying provider, anywhere in our network, Netlify’s service would continue with minimal interruption. Our origin services can now swap between three providers: Google Cloud (GCP), AWS, and Rackspace Cloud without downtime. This post will cover how we planed, tested, and executed our first multi-cloud migration Planning for change The main goal for this project was to have a multi-cloud production system where we could direct traffic to different providers on demand, without interruptions. Our primary sources of data are the database and the cloud store — the first for keeping references to the data and the second for the data itself. To keep latency down, we needed to run a production-ready copy of both sources in every provider. They also needed to have automatic fallbacks configured to the other clouds. For example, Google instances prioritize Google Cloud Storage (GCS) and fallback to S3 automatically. We first built a tool called cloud bench that would check the performance of uploads to different cloud storages. It showed us what we suspected: upload to a cloud storage was faster if it stayed in the same provider. We also confirmed that pricing was better if uploads stayed inside the same network. We went through the different services that touched the data in the cloud provider, extracting simple Get/Put interfaces for that data and implementing concrete versions for Google, Amazon, and Rackspace. We then released the service, with the abstracted interface, that would use Rackspace — our current cloud provider. Then we started to test that service with the different implementations for the other clouds. AWS and GCP offer more robust load balancers than what we were using. Rackspace is limited to around 10GB/s, which is a lot under normal operation, but not in the event of DDoS. Both Google and Amazon don’t place any limits, saying that the frontend load balancers will scale up as needed to support the traffic. Data Replication Netlify customers have deployed terabytes of data and they’re deploying more every day. Before the migration, all of this data was stored in a single service: Rackspace’s Cloudfiles. Our first challenge was to build a system able to replicate the millions of blob objects we stored and start replicating new data as it came in. Our approach attached a bitmask to the object reference that indicated where it was replicated. We did this to keep down the bloat on the database as there are millions of entries and adding long strings to each would balloon the database size. It also meant that any service that needed to use that blob now knew from where it could load the data. This bitmask opened the way for intelligent prioritization in different services. We built a Go service that would inspect an existing blob, figure out where it needed to push it to, actually push it, and record its progress. The service was able to act in both online replication and batch backfilling modes. We fed a few million objects to the service for replication. After manually checking those blobs, we started two processes. One that would process newly-uploaded objects and one to backfill the existing objects. We chose a passive replication strategy for the objects; the service would come through and clean up from time to time. A more active strategy, like a 3-phase commit, introduced risk into the upload phase. For instance, bugs or provider issues could slow or disable uploads completely. It is also a simpler change in our system as it didn’t impact the request chain at all. We could iterate on the service with minimal risk to the primary flow. There is only a small fraction of objects that aren’t replicated in the event that we swap providers. Objects are available across providers and the system automatically handles that. Recovery The system is flexible enough to handle recovering quickly; we’d take degraded performance over an outage any day. Traffic can be quickly redirected internally by updating service configurations. We can direct traffic to any of our clouds, including splitting traffic, in order to keep from dropping requests. Of course there are cost and performance considerations when doing this, especially when crossing cloud boundaries, but uptime is the priority. Just the other day we had to configure a cross cloud setup. We detected a latency issue in our Google integration and manually intervened to swap reads from S3 while we investigated. Once we worked out the kinks with the integration we returned the configuration to its resting state, preferring the cloud the service was in. Doing things manually is often too slow.
sampled: Since January 1, 2017, AMZN shares rose 91% while GOOGL shares rose only 41%, a gap that reflects meaningfully different investor confidence in the two companies over that stretch. The divergence became even sharper after fourth-quarter earnings, when the market delivered a blunt verdict on each company's trajectory. After 4Q results, AMZN shares rose 3%, adding nearly $20 billion in market cap, while GOOGL shares fell 5%, removing over $40 billion from Alphabet's market cap. Those moves in opposite directions captured a broader anxiety that had been building around Google's cost structure and its ability to defend margins. A central concern for GOOGL heading into and through 4Q was continued negative surprises in operating profit margin, driven specifically by higher traffic acquisition costs, known as TAC. These costs represent what Google pays to distribution partners to secure search placement, and they had been climbing faster than many on Wall Street anticipated. Analyst James Dix had flagged this pressure early, publishing a report titled "A Closer Look Reveals Sites TAC Pressures Could Be Worse Than Expected" in February of the prior year. That report proved prescient: a year before it appeared, Wall Street expected Sites TAC as a percentage of revenue to rise by about 1 percentage point over 2017, while Dix predicted more than twice that, and the actual increase came in even greater. GOOGL management responded to the TAC concern by guiding investors toward a slower pace of growth in Sites TAC percentage after the first quarter of 2018, citing visibility from multi-year distribution agreements already in place. That guidance offered some reassurance, though the damage to sentiment from the 4Q miss had already registered in the stock price. One reason Google commands such high distribution costs is the sheer scale of its search dominance, which gives partners leverage to extract payments for default placement. According to Merkle, GOOGL held 92% of U.S. search traffic overall and 96% on mobile in 4Q, numbers that illustrate both the strength of the franchise and the cost of maintaining it. Despite heavy investment in non-advertising products like Google Home and Pixel, advertising still accounted for 86% of GOOGL's revenue in 2017. That figure, while down from 92% in 2013, shows how thoroughly Google's revenue base remains tied to a single business model even after years of diversification effort. The profit picture is even more concentrated than the revenue mix suggests. GOOGL's profit contribution from advertising, though not formally disclosed, is estimated to be nearly 100%, meaning the rest of the company's product portfolio generates little to no meaningful earnings. GOOGL's operating margin stood at 23.7% in 4Q and 23.6% for the full year 2017, numbers that look healthy in isolation but carry risk when the underlying revenue source is so narrowly defined. Any structural pressure on advertising economics therefore flows almost directly into the company's bottom line with little buffer from other segments. Amazon's financial profile looks strikingly different. AMZN's operating margins were 3.5% in 4Q and just 1.0% for the full year 2017, reflecting a business that deliberately reinvests at a pace that suppresses reported profits in exchange for long-term scale and market position. Amazon's advertising business, contained within its other net sales category, was likely up approximately 60% year-over-year in 4Q, pointing to a fast-growing revenue stream that could eventually challenge Google's dominance in certain advertising formats. That growth sits inside a company whose e-commerce and cloud operations give it multiple ways to generate value independent of ad revenue. Amazon Prime bundles subscription benefits with e-commerce convenience in a way that builds deep consumer loyalty and recurring revenue, a model that differs fundamentally from Google's reliance on attention-based advertising. Netflix competes with Amazon Prime on the subscription video side, but Amazon's broader ecosystem gives Prime a stickiness that pure streaming services cannot replicate. James Dix argues that tokenization will pose a greater long-term threat to GOOGL's economics than to AMZN's, and he cites three reasons for that view. The core logic is that Google's business depends on harvesting consumer data and attention in ways that blockchain-based token models could directly disrupt by redirecting value back to users. The combined market cap of tokens from a sample of blockchains promising to transfer value to consumers for use of their data is approximately $4 billion, a figure that remains small relative to Google's scale but signals where developer and investor attention is pointing. If those models gain traction, the implicit exchange that funds Google's advertising business could face meaningful renegotiation. Amazon's revenue model, by contrast, is grounded in transactional commerce and cloud infrastructure rather than the data-for-attention exchange that tokenization most directly challenges. That structural difference is part of why Dix views AMZN as less exposed to the tokenization threat than GOOGL over a longer time horizon. The contrast between the two companies extends beyond business model risk to the question of where each earns its profits. Google's near-total profit dependence on advertising creates a single point of vulnerability that Amazon, with its diversified operating segments, does not share in the same way. The 4Q results served as a concrete illustration of how quickly investor sentiment can shift when a company's cost structure surprises to the downside, even for a business as dominant as Google. Losing over $40 billion in market cap in the wake of a single earnings report underscores how sensitive the stock remains to any sign that TAC pressures are outpacing management's ability to control them. Both companies enter subsequent quarters carrying the weight of these divergent narratives: Amazon rewarded for growth and reinvestment, Alphabet scrutinized for margin discipline and the durability of an advertising model that still generates nearly all of its profit. The 50-percentage-point gap in share price performance since January 1, 2017 reflects how differently the market has chosen to price those two stories.

original: Why Test? The majority of ads will fail. So unless you’re expecting a neverending streak of luck, you’ll need a process for separating the losers from the winners. That’s where A/B testing comes in. It’s simply the process of testing two or more ad variations against each other, analyzing the results, and doing less of what doesn’t work & more of what works. It’s hard to overstate how important this is. We frequently see ads perform 2x, 5x or even 10x better than others. And the first ads are almost never among the top performers. So if you’re not running at least one test at any given time, you’re leaving money on the table. What To Test First, you’ll need a bunch of copy angles and creatives. This is a huge topic in and of itself, so we won’t get into it here. Let’s just assume you have them. Great! Where do you start? You’ll want to go as BIG as possible with the first test. An example would be testing a professionally shot studio photo vs an unedited UGC (User Generated Content) video, or short CTA-focused ad copy vs long-form storytelling copy. The more contrast you add, the easier it will be to analyze the results and hone in one the winning angles. We like to start things off with a 2 x 2: two creatives and two copy. We find that this strikes a good balance between simplicity and effectiveness. 2 x 2 Is An Easy Way To Get Started The results from the first test determine what we do next. For instance, let’s say we find that there was a huge difference in performance between the creatives but no real difference between the copy variations. We would then isolate that variable, i.e. test a handful of creatives with the same copy. If you’ve got a large budget and want to be as hands-off as possible, you can use Facebook’s Dynamic Creative. It does work and we do use it, but most times we prefer to have more control. When To Test When it comes to testing, we believe that frequency is more important than volume. It’s better to run multiple tests with a few variations, then a few tests with multiple variations. That’s why we use a two-day testing cycle. On any given ad account we’re analyzing and implementing new ad copy and creative up to three times per week (Monday, Wednesday, Friday). Usually, the number of tests you can run is limited by the budget. But even on the accounts where we’re not able to test new variations every two days, we still analyze and monitor performance. Note: Adding a new ad to an existing ad set will reset the learning phase. It may make sense to use a designated campaign for testing. How To Test Analyzing the results is maybe the most challenging part. There’s a lot that goes into the analysis, but there are a couple of simple tools that can do most of the heavy lifting. Having a simple process is extremely helpful for removing emotion and making informed decisions quickly. We like to use this decision tree (credit: https://commonthreadco.com) as a guide. Ad Kill Decision Tree In order to be able to use the decision tree, you’ll need to have target CPAs for all correlated variables. Here’s a document that will help you with that. When needed, we also use a Significance Calculator. A/B Testing Like A Scientist You simply plug in the numbers and the calculator tells you how confident you can be that any difference in performance is real and not due to random variation. Since the whole point of Facebook’s targeting is to move away from random sampling, this obviously isn’t a perfect tool. But it’s useful as a reality check. After The Test The results from the test are documented and handed over to the creative team. We use a simple scoring scale (Poor, Okay, Good) and qualitative comments. Scoring the ads can be more art than science, given the many factors involved. That’s why it’s best done by a media buyer who spends a lot of time in the ad account. In Summary By the time you’re reading this, we may have made a few (or many) changes to our A/B testing process. Nevertheless, the general principles and concepts apply. Good luck!
sampled: Harry Hogg re-read his wife's first letter after many long years, and the experience of holding those pages again carried the full weight of a shared life that had quietly accumulated between the lines of her handwriting and the places she described. The two of them had been childhood sweethearts, which means that the story running through those letters was not simply a romance but something closer to a parallel growing-up, a record of two people who had known each other before they knew themselves. What strikes Hogg most, looking back, is that love letters rather than teachers gave him the ability to write at all, shaping his sense of language through the intimate pressure of wanting to be understood by one specific person across whatever distance separated them. His wife wrote many of those letters with the sound of the sea close by, and that proximity to water gave her words a particular quality, a kind of open, unhurried attention to the world around her that he found himself reaching toward in his own prose. Most of Hogg's life was lived near the sea as well, and he acknowledges that this shared geography shows in his writing, lending it a texture that is harder to arrive at through craft alone and easier to absorb simply by spending years listening to the rhythm of tides against a familiar shoreline. The couple shared a love of the written word and a deep appreciation for their part of the world, which meant that even the most ordinary letters between them carried a kind of mutual recognition, a sense that both people were paying close attention to the same things. The letters Hogg loved most were the ones that spoke of his wife's feeling for their home and garden, because those letters grounded the romance in something physical and tended, something that required daily care rather than only emotion, and that combination of feeling and practical devotion gave the correspondence a texture no purely passionate letter could match. He describes a span of forty years from the birth of their first child to the present moment of her absence, and that number carries the essay's central weight, marking the distance between a beginning that felt full of possibility and a present that holds only the evidence of what was built. Hogg places the letter under blue and white Anemones and looks out at a misty shoreline, and the image works not as decoration but as a precise record of where he is sitting and what surrounds him at the moment of re-reading, grounding the emotional experience in a specific, visible place. The green and yellow he paints the house, described as his wife's favorite color scheme, belongs to the same logic of tending, of keeping the physical world aligned with her preferences even now, which is a form of fidelity that requires no words at all. The couple found Glasgow too tough and preferred Paris, and that preference says something concrete about the kind of life they were drawn toward, one that favored a certain ease of beauty over industrial hardness, a city where the written word and lingering over things felt less out of place. Hogg mentions choosing La Perla underwear from the lingerie sections of shops, a detail that lands in the essay as evidence of attentiveness, of the small acts of selection that accumulate over decades into a portrait of someone you have studied carefully enough to know their taste without being told. The letters also mentioned Rome and Amsterdam and Ruth and Knud's bar, places and names that carried their own histories and gave the correspondence a geographical breadth, a sense that the couple's inner life was not confined to one location but had been tested and enriched across different cities and encounters. That breadth makes the return to the home and garden letters all the more telling, because after all the travel and variety, what his wife chose to write about with the most feeling was the particular patch of world they had made together. Hogg's essay turns on the idea that a single line could sum up a life together, and the impossibility of finding that line is not a failure but a measure of how much the life contained, how resistant it is to compression without loss.

original: What to Buy (and What to Skip) to Prepare for Coronavirus Advice from people in quarantine about what you actually need — and how to make life work Photo: Universal Images Group/Getty Images Follow Elemental’s ongoing coverage of the coronavirus outbreak here. The World Health Organization has officially declared Covid-19 a pandemic, and if you’ve been hoping you can ignore coronavirus and it’ll just go away without affecting you or your family in some way, that’s looking less and less likely. But that isn’t to say you need to buy a deep freezer and build a storehouse in your backyard. So where should you begin, and how can you approach preparation without driving yourself up the wall? The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has offered up guidance on how to prepare for an outbreak near you, including making a plan with your family, practicing good health and hygiene habits, and checking in with vulnerable people in your community. They also have instructed people in at-risk groups (like the immunocompromised, the elderly, and those with chronic health conditions) to stock up on supplies like nonperishable foods. Since things are moving quickly, it’s not a bad idea to stock up a bit before the virus hits your area, since social distancing (which can include limiting your visits to, say, crowded supermarkets and pharmacies) is such a helpful preventive measure, and you may need to self-quarantine with limited notice. In case you do have to hole up for a while, here’s what you may need to make it, well, suck less — based on advice from experts and folks who’ve actually been in quarantine. There’s already been a run on toilet paper and paper towels — for good reason. A sensible grocery list “It’s about stocking your pantry in a smart way, but also cooking with the stuff you already have in the house,” says Dawn Perry, a food writer who’s currently working on a pantry cookbook. Here’s her quick-and-dirty rundown of what you may need, including staples and flavor boosters so you’re not just stuck eating black beans out of a can: Dry grains: Rice, quinoa, oats, cornmeal (for polenta). Beans: dried or canned. Tinned fish: tuna, tasty cans of smoked sardines, or mackerel. A couple varieties of nut butter and tahini. Flour (you can add water, salt, and a leavening agent like baking soda or powder to make biscuits, tortillas, and crackers). Eggs. Onions (they keep for weeks when stored in a cool, dark place). Garlic. Potatoes. Boxed cereal. Hardy veggies: broccoli, celery, carrots, and kale (they stay fresh for a long time in your fridge). Bananas (when they start to turn, freeze for smoothies or bake into banana bread). Frozen peas (add to soups and pastas). Frozen sausage (just one link can go a long way in adding flavor to a dish). Bag of frozen shrimp. Sliced bread (pop it in your freezer, will last a long time). Taste boosters: soy sauce, mayo, ketchup, fruit jam, Dijon mustard, Parmesan cheese, olives, capers. First aid kit No matter what is happening — pandemic or regular day — “it’s prudent for every household to have basic essentials on hand to care for a minor emergency, such as a cut, burn, or insect sting,” says Brad Uren, MD, assistant professor of emergency medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School. (And while you should, of course, seek medical care if you need it, for minor issues you can treat at home, it’s preferable not to visit a health care facility right now if you don’t have to.) A standard first aid kit will have what you need. Extra supply of needed medication Make sure you have a few weeks of vital medications on hand, says Uren. Mail-order pharmacies, which often dole out 90-day supplies when available, may be an option for certain people, depending on what type of medication they’re taking and insurance, he says. If you’re having trouble making this happen (insurance doesn’t always make it easy), get on the phone with a pharmacist. OTC meds and other symptom treatments Should you get sick, you’ll want to have the right supplies on hand to treat your symptoms, says Aaron Reddington of the survival blog the Simple Prepper. Make sure you have things like a thermometer, OTC fever reducers (acetaminophen and ibuprofen), sports drinks for rehydrating, and the bland foods you want when you have no appetite, like crackers, he says. Hygiene stuff There’s already been a run on toilet paper and paper towels — for good reason. “While everyone has reacted and bought toilet paper and paper towels, unfortunately, I think you need to roll with the punches and buy some as well,” says Reddington. “It would be terrible to be stuck in your home for weeks without any, and while it may sound ridiculous [to stock up], worst-case scenario is that you have extra,” he says.
sampled: Pascal Barry's argument about design systems is a pointed one: that these widely celebrated tools are, at their core, harmful to design practice and the creativity that good design demands. The case he builds draws on research across more than 200 articles on Medium and other blogs, a volume of reading that shapes a skeptical and carefully reasoned position. The argument finds a useful parallel in Natasha Jen's 2018 talk "Design Thinking Is Bullsh*t," where she observed that "In today's world design has become this box that people just want to check off." Barry sees design systems operating in exactly that spirit, reducing a complex discipline to something that can be ticked off a project checklist. Brad Frost's definition of a design system offers a revealing starting point for the critique. Frost wrote that "A kit of UI components without accompanying philosophy, principles, guidelines, processes, and documentation is like dumping a bunch of IKEA components on the floor and saying 'Here, build a dresser!'" Barry finds this analogy itself troubling rather than reassuring. The IKEA comparison, meant to underscore what design systems need to succeed, inadvertently exposes what they assume: that design is a matter of assembly rather than judgment. Barry argues this framing devalues design by making it appear fully actionable by people who are not designers at all. One practical consequence of that devaluation is organizational. Barry contends that design systems tend to be adopted only by the designers who created them, while the broader teams they were meant to serve either ignore them or find them irrelevant to their actual working conditions. This echoes a point made in a piece titled "Design systems in difficult places," where an unnamed contributor observed that "The challenge with any design system is they normally don't work, don't get adopted, don't grow or get used if they are imposed top-down without an awful lot of consultation." The gap between a system's ambition and its uptake is rarely acknowledged by its advocates. Barry's own professional history gives the argument a grounded texture. He worked at a startup that went through multiple rebrands and product pivots within its first three years, an environment where any rigid system would have become a liability rather than a foundation. That kind of rapid change is common in early-stage product development, and it exposes a structural problem with design systems. When design is fused tightly with code, changes to the product are slowed or quietly discouraged because the cost of updating the system feels too high. The single-point-of-failure problem compounds this. A bug introduced into a shared design system does not stay contained; it propagates across every product touch point that draws from the same source, multiplying the damage in ways that a more distributed approach would not permit. Barry draws a comparison between design systems and corporate brand guidelines, describing both as equally tedious and equally ignored in practice. The parallel is deliberate: brand guidelines were supposed to enforce consistency too, and they largely failed to do so for the same reasons. The deeper issue is one of values. Barry argues that design systems prioritize consistency and convenience at the expense of creativity and craft, trading the harder qualities of good design for the easier ones that are simpler to document and enforce. His alternative centers on coherence rather than consistency. Coherence, in his framing, allows for contextual deviations where a design decision serves the specific moment rather than the system's rules, producing work that feels considered rather than templated. The GOV.UK Design System serves as a telling case study in the difficulty of making these systems actually function. Its contribution model took 2 years to develop and was still not complete, a timeline that illustrates how much invisible labor design systems demand beyond their initial build. Barry's preferred values form a clear set of priorities: communication over documentation, craft over convenience, creativity over uniformity, coherence over consistency, and context over everything else. Each pairing names what design systems tend to suppress in favor of what they reward. The documentation problem is particularly pointed. Design systems generate enormous amounts of written guidance, but Barry's framework treats communication as the real goal, something that documentation can obstruct when it becomes the primary artifact of design work. Craft is similarly crowded out. When components are pre-built and decisions are pre-made, the designer's role shifts from making considered choices to selecting from an approved menu, a change that Barry sees as a meaningful erosion of what design actually is. Nassim Taleb's thinking about fragility and systems informs Barry's broader skepticism. A system designed for efficiency and uniformity can become brittle precisely because it has removed the variation and redundancy that allow for resilience under real conditions. The argument does not call for chaos or the abandonment of shared tools. It calls for honesty about what design systems cost: the creative friction they eliminate, the contextual judgment they override, and the false sense of order they produce in organizations that still need designers to think.

original: There are 13 days left before the writing part of the Blog-Your-Own-Book Challenge starts. I’m going to give you homework tonight that you might hate me for now, but you’ll really thank me for it later. First, a story. I’m a novelist. Before my first novel was published, I wrote three novels that were not. I was a straight-up pantser when I wrote those books. I was sure plotting would eat my story’s soul. That it would make it impossible for me to write my book the way I wanted to. After my first novel was published, my editor did something that changed the way I write forever. She asked me to send her a synopsis for a novel I hadn’t written yet. And she expected it by the end of the month. I had to learn to plot. Fast. I did and the result was a book that A) was the best thing I’d written up to that date and B) I was able to write in one quarter of the time I was used to taking. One quarter. I’ve plotted every book I’ve ever written since then. I’ve never looked back. The PSST Framework is Like Blog-Post Plotting All of that is to say that I use a framework for my blog posts for the same reason I plot my novels. It’s faster. It’s so much easier. And, it turns out, it’s actually pretty fun. I like thinking about my blog posts and imagining what they might be. PSST stands for Premise, Story, Subheads, and Take-away. I actually have a page in my Rocketbook that I used a Sharpie on to make a form that I literally fill out before I write each post. The PSST page in my Rocketbook. Photo: Author I use a Frixion pen to fill out the form for every post. A little water erases it, but leaves the Sharpie template. If I end up not actually writing my post that day or I want to create a bunch of PSST forms for posts, I just take a picture of them. Like the one above, which is for a post I didn’t actually write. Yet. The parts are so simple. Let me break it down for you. Premise Premise is just a ‘p’ for ‘working title’ — because I thought PSST Framework was cute. Just write what your post is about in a few words. Don’t be cute or clever. Think newspaper headline. You need to be able to look back on your post framework and know what you were wanting to talk about. This is a good exercise, too, because simple, clear, concise titles do well for blog posts. Story I firmly believe that every every blog post should start with a story. In the first ‘S’ box on my form, I write a sentence or two about which story I’ll tell in that particular post. I write enough to remind myself of the story I want to tell, but really only a few words. I don’t spend too much time here and I pretty much never second guess myself. If I get ready to write and a better story comes to me, I write that one instead. But most of the time, my instincts are pretty good. I bet yours are, too. We’re storytellers. Trust that. Subheads This is pretty much the body of your post in a series of sentences. Just think about what you want to say about your premise. It helps me to ask myself ‘what is the first thing some one needs to know’ and then I ask ‘and then what’ until I reach the end. Take-Away Your take-away is the way you end your post. What do you want your readers to take from it? What do you want them to do after they read your post? How do you want to change them? Your Homework Okay, so a few days ago I asked you to come up with your 31 posts for your BYOB Project.
sampled: Data journalism sits at the intersection of reporting and rigorous quantitative analysis, drawing on a discipline that Alex Howard defined as "gathering, cleaning, organizing, analyzing, visualizing and publishing data to support the creation of acts of journalism." That definition captures something important: the work is not simply about having numbers on hand but about moving those numbers through a structured process that ends in a story the public can understand and use. The practice has roots that stretch back much further than most people assume, with Florence Nightingale producing influential data-driven work in 1858 and John Snow completing his now-famous Cholera Visualization around the same period. Both figures demonstrated that carefully collected and clearly presented data could shift public understanding in ways that conventional narrative reporting alone could not accomplish, making them early models for what the field would eventually become. Ben Casselman of the New York Times has articulated the practical value of data for working journalists in concrete terms, noting that data helps journalists verify claims, tackle bigger stories, find new stories, illuminate murky issues, and report more efficiently. Those five functions cover a wide range of editorial situations, from the quick fact-check that prevents a published error to the long investigation that exposes a systemic problem hidden inside thousands of rows of records. One honest characterization of the data journalism process describes it as 80% perspiration, 10% great ideas, and 10% output, a ratio that reflects how much of the work happens before any story is written or any chart is published. The bulk of the effort goes into locating, cleaning, and checking data, and that labor-intensive phase is precisely what separates a credible data story from one built on shaky foundations. Datasets themselves can come from very different places: some arrive ready-made through government portals or research institutions, while others must be constructed by extracting information from multimedia files, conducting interviews, or carrying out original analysis and research. The choice of source shapes everything that follows, because data gathered through interviews carries different reliability considerations than data downloaded from an official statistical agency, and both types require the journalist to think carefully about provenance. The Guardian has noted that data is not a force unto itself, does not speak for itself, is not power by itself, is not a perfect reflection of the world, and is not easy to interpret, a list of cautions that pushes back against the idea that numbers are inherently authoritative. Alongside that warning sits the related fact that not all official data sources are reliable, accurate, or correct, which means the credibility of a source's institutional standing cannot substitute for independent verification of the data itself. Mona Chalabi described her own editorial filter for deciding when a data-driven piece is worth pursuing: "I ask myself whether the numbers I'm looking at will start a new conversation that people aren't having yet, or if they will add to an existing conversation in a valuable way. If the answer to both of those questions is no, then I don't bother to write the piece." That standard keeps the focus on genuine public value rather than on the novelty of having data available. Once the analysis is complete, visualization becomes a critical stage in its own right, requiring deliberate decisions about colors, graph types, and scales that can dramatically change how readers perceive the underlying information. Tools such as Tableau, Power BI, Python, and R each offer different capabilities for this stage, and the choice among them depends on the complexity of the dataset, the technical capacity of the newsroom, and the format in which the final piece will be published. The data journalism process can unfold as either a long investigative effort or a shorter one that covers only the key data points a story requires, meaning the discipline is not reserved for large teams with months of runway. Whether the project runs for weeks or a few days, the same core obligations apply: find reliable data, interrogate its limitations honestly, and present the findings in a form that readers can actually follow and evaluate.

original: The Simplest Form of Mindfulness Is Also the Most Effective Most of us are cognitively aware that our bad habits are, well, BAD. The challenge is that our prefrontal cortex (front section of the brain) that is responsible for this awareness is the first to go offline when we get stressed. When this brain center logs off, we start to feel ‘numb’, give in to our stress, and fall back onto negative habits. Let’s go back to the 3 pillars that form a habit one more time. You experience a trigger. You respond with a behavior. You receive a reward. Say you’re battling the urge to have that fourth slice of pizza. You’ve already experienced the trigger that’s telling you, “Yes, this is a great idea…you’ll feel so good after”. What if we took a split second here to pause before caving in? What if we were to use curiosity as a tool to disrupt the cycle? Here’s what it looks like: You feel a trigger that spurs temptation. Instead of caving in, you pause for a moment and get curious. Ask yourself…what’s going on? Why am I feeling this way? From here you have two possible routes, both of which are a step in the right direction. The first path is that you still give in to your bad behavior, but with a heightened state of mindfulness. The act of caving in feels much less satisfying. You become consciously aware that the reward is just a guise covering up the reality that you’re in an endless loop of going nowhere. In one of Brewers’s studies, a subject involved with smoking admitted that mindful smoking, “smells like stinky cheese, and tastes like chemicals, YUCK!”. This paper eventually reveals that mindfulness training may confer benefits greater than those associated with current standard treatments for smoking cessation. No money, drugs, or therapy required. The second route is when things get really exciting. This is when you experience the trigger, but you’re now inherently aware that this is a poor choice and you take a halt. This is how you move from knowledge to wisdom. We’re all cognitively aware that bad habits aren’t good for us. Curiosity bridges the gap to allow us to be mindful of this, even when we’re stressed out or ‘in the act’. When you start to implement this curiosity technique into your behaviors, bad habits simply become less enchanting. You start to wise up and realize that you don’t need to give in to every trigger that comes your way. An amazing bonus to this mindset is that curiosity in itself is rewarding. Being mindful amidst your stressed-out state will deliver the prize that you were initially seeking from your ‘drug’ of choice. It may not be as powerful of a hit, but over time, your brain will realize that it’s the one you need. This is a rewarding, sustainable, and life-changing way to think about human behavior. Will it solve all of your problems instantly? Absolutely not. Many addictions are as much physiological as they are psychological. At times, it may be necessary to get professional help. Regardless, this is a powerful tool for initiating an important conversation with yourself. It is one that empowers you to ditch the dissociation and start attacking your bad habits head-on.
sampled: Faith is not a license to treat people badly. Crystal Jackson, writing from the southern United States, argues that many religious people have centered their faith around hate rather than love. She observes this pattern most clearly in Christianity, where the loudest voices often seem more invested in judgment than in the grace their tradition claims to prize. The gap between what a religion teaches and how its followers behave is not a small one. Jackson defines a "Jesus card" as the belief that a religious identity gives someone a pass to behave badly toward others. No such pass exists. No tradition grants it. No scripture supports it. She points to Galatians 5:22-23, which lists the fruits of the spirit as love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. These are not suggestions tucked away in a footnote but the described markers of a life shaped by faith. The list does not include contempt. It does not include cruelty. The argument is not confined to Christianity alone. Jackson traces a shared ethical principle across multiple traditions, finding the same core instruction repeated in Buddhism, Confucianism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism, and Native American Spirituality. The principle holds across centuries. It holds across continents. Matthew 7:12 in the King James Version states, "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them." This is the Christian articulation of the Golden Rule, and it leaves no room for carve-outs based on who the other person is or what they believe. The Islamic version appears as Number 13 of Al-Nawawi's Forty Hadiths, attributed to Muhammad, and carries the same weight. The Hindu tradition draws the same boundary at Mahabharata 5:1517. Leviticus 19:18 puts the Jewish version plainly: "Thou shalt love thy neighbor as thyself." The Buddhist tradition sources a parallel instruction at Udana-Varga 5:18. Across all of these, the number of traditions that carve out an exception for cruelty is zero. Jackson notes that even Satanists hold standards around treating others with compassion, which makes the behavior of some self-identified Christians harder to excuse. The presence of that standard across traditions, including ones most Christians would reject outright, undercuts any claim that faith justifies contempt. The Great Law of Peace, cited as the Native American Spirituality articulation of the same principle, states, "Respect for all life is the foundation." That framing does not leave room for conditional respect, the kind that applies only to people who look, believe, or live the way you do. Jackson takes the cross-traditional consistency of this principle seriously. Jackson does not position herself as someone who has always gotten this right. She acknowledges personal moments of being guilty of treating others poorly, which keeps the essay from reading as a simple indictment of other people. The article was published on Medium on October 8, 2019, and the argument it makes draws on verse references from Galatians 5:22-23, Matthew 7:12, Leviticus 19:18, Mahabharata 5:1517, and Udana-Varga 5:18 to show that the Golden Rule is not a Christian invention but a human one. No tradition listed grants its followers permission to be unkind. Jackson's core claim is that faith, when used as a weapon against others, has been separated from its own roots.

original: When You Feel like You Can’t Live up to Your Own Writing Late night self-reflections of a writer on book deadline A page from my journal that night. I was rolling around in bed at 2 am. My mind was racing with outstanding tasks, unwritten paragraphs, and self-doubt. Together with my co-author John Fitch I’m in the final stages of writing a book about the importance of Time Off. And we are on a rapidly approaching deadline to hand the draft over to our editor. Many authors I talked to in the past told me that they are a mental mess in the days before handing off their manuscript, but I hoped I’d be immune to this. Especially given the topic we are writing about. But there I was, unable to sleep because my mind couldn’t stop worrying about the book. And at a deeper layer, worrying about the worrying. So I did the only thing I could think of at the moment to calm down my mind. I got up and put my thoughts to paper, writing the following words in my notebook to reassure myself of what I am doing. It helped me a lot. Maybe if you are in a similar situation, it can help you too.
sampled: Code review is one of the most debated practices in software engineering, yet its core purpose is often misunderstood. Nick Bull wrote a guide on what code review is actually meant to accomplish. The piece appeared in Better Programming, a publication on Medium. It was published on October 23, 2020, and draws on best practices from 5 major tech companies. Those companies are Apple, Google, Microsoft, Amazon, and Facebook. Many engineers treat code review as a checklist exercise, focused on confirming that changes work, that style guides are followed, and that no regressions have been introduced. Bull argues that while those checks matter, they are not the point of the process. The real purpose, according to Bull, is to ensure the solution solves the problem in the best possible way, taking into account both code quality and product considerations. That framing shifts code review from a gatekeeping task into a collaborative problem-solving conversation. Checking for regressions and style guide adherence are considered necessary parts of the review, but treating them as the goal misses the broader function that code review serves.

original: In honor of my birthday coming up, I decided it might be fun to bestow what little wisdom I have. You’re probably wondering why you should listen to the ramblings of a 20-year-old? Well, me too. Hopefully, there is something here for you. In 20 years I’ve had the pleasure (and often displeasure) of learning some hard lessons. 1. Don’t Settle Don’t go for junk food when you can easily cook a healthy meal that will boost your mood and immune system. Don’t settle for the guy who doesn’t answer when you call. Don’t settle for fake friends. Don’t settle for anything less than you deserve. 2. Be Yourself It took me longer than I’d like to admit to learn this one, but I’ve always struggled with showing people a version of me, that well… wasn’t me. Always put your best self forward, and never let anyone make you feel bad for who you are. 3. Work Smarter… and Harder I’m all for finding an easier way to accomplish a task, but I’m also a firm believer in you get what you put in. Never lose sight of your end goals, and always put in 110% effort. 4. Your Journey is Yours Never let someone else’s life make you feel like you’re behind on yours. Everyone moves at their own pace. Some people may graduate college in 3 years, some may graduate in 8. You’ll reach your goals when you’re meant to. 5. Relax and Enjoy Speaking of your journey, enjoy it! Life is to short to only focus on the bad. You’ll be a lot happier if you relish in the good things. 6. Loosen Your Grip No one, in the entire world, has control over every aspect of their life. There may be some people that portray that image, but it’s an act. Focus on what you can control, and let go of what you can’t. 7. Family Isn’t Always Blood You don’t have to be related to have a family bond with someone. The people who stick by you through the good, the bad, and the ugly can be better for you than your blood relatives. 8. You Lose Some, You Gain Some People come, and people go. If they want to leave, let them. 9. Turn Rejection Into Motivation You’re going to face a lot of rejection in this lifetime so you might as well use it for good. Take every “no,” and let it push you to work harder. 10. We Aren’t All The Same, and That’s Okay You’re going to meet people that disagree with you. They’re going to disagree on small things, they’re going to disagree on huge, fundamental, things. It’s okay to disagree without fighting. 11. Be Kind This one’s a little cheesy, but it’s so true. Simple kindnesses make a big difference in other people’s lives and a big difference in yours. Never forget, you get what you give. 12. Give Yourself Permission To Be Lazy Every once in awhile we all need to lay around and do absolutely nothing. Don’t feel bad for letting yourself rest, but don’t forget to pick yourself up off the couch the next day and get back to work. 13. Your Opinion is King Not everyone is going to like you or the things you do. It doesn’t matter. If you’re happy, then it’s right for you. Don’t let other people control your happiness. 14. Read as Much as You Can Reading can change your life and change your mindset. Even if you hate reading, listen to an audiobook. There’s so much in this life to learn and experience. Books are a cheap vacation in another world. 15. Jump At The Chance To Learn Take that online course, go back to college, listen to an educational podcast, watch the news. Every time you have an opportunity to learn something, take it. It will help you grow and allow you to help others. 16.
sampled: Procrastination stands out as one of the biggest challenges people face when trying to stay productive each day, and the problem is not simply a matter of poor planning or bad habits. Renata Gomes argues that discipline and willpower are far more reliable tools for beating procrastination than waiting around for inspiration or motivation to arrive on their own. The reasoning behind this position becomes clearer when you consider how motivation tends to fluctuate without warning, making it an unstable foundation for consistent work. Discipline, by contrast, operates independently of how a person feels on a given morning, which is precisely why Gomes treats it as the more dependable of the two forces. One concept that sheds light on why procrastination takes hold so easily is Parkinson's law, which holds that "work expands so as to fill the time available for its completion." A task that would normally take three hours can quietly stretch to fill an entire week if a week is what has been allotted for it. Gomes characterizes Parkinson's law as sitting closer to a humorous saying than to a scientifically proven principle, placing it in a different category from Newton's laws of physics or even the more tongue-in-cheek Murphy's law. Still, the observation carries practical weight because most people have experienced exactly this kind of time expansion in their own work lives. The core remedy Gomes proposes is a simple 10-minute exercise that involves setting a timer and working exclusively on a chosen task for that entire duration without stopping. The exercise originated as a creative writing technique, but Gomes is clear that it can be adapted to suit many other kinds of work beyond writing. Gomes first encountered this 10-minute approach in a creative writing class, where it was used to push writers past the inertia that so often accompanies a blank page. The fact that the technique transferred well from that specific context into broader productivity advice suggests its value is not tied to any single type of task. The rules during those 10 minutes are strict: checking a phone is not allowed, and browsing the internet is equally off-limits for the duration. Removing those distractions is not incidental to the exercise but central to it, because the goal is to create a brief window of complete, undivided attention on one thing. What makes the exercise particularly interesting is what tends to happen once the timer goes off and the 10 minutes are finished. Gomes claims that momentum typically carries the person forward, keeping them working well beyond the point where they were technically free to stop. That observation about momentum connects to a broader point about how starting is usually the hardest part of any task, and how a short, low-stakes commitment can quietly dissolve the resistance that procrastination feeds on. Once the initial friction is gone, continuing feels far less effortful than it did before the timer was set. Deadlines play a related role in this framework, and Gomes describes both self-imposed and external deadlines as genuinely helpful for boosting productivity. Whether the deadline comes from a manager or from a personal commitment written in a notebook, the effect of a time constraint on output is real and worth deliberately engineering. The pomodoro technique is mentioned as a popular productivity strategy that shares some structural similarities with the 10-minute exercise, particularly in its use of timed intervals to organize focused work. Both approaches treat time limits not as pressure but as a practical mechanism for making work feel more contained and therefore more approachable. Taken together, these ideas point toward a view of productivity that relies on structure rather than mood, and on concrete time constraints rather than open-ended stretches of available hours. The 10-minute exercise, Parkinson's law, and the role of deadlines all reinforce the same underlying logic: that the shape of the time given to a task has a direct effect on how that task actually gets done.

original: When your data needs to get dressed up, Tableau is a fool-proof style service. It offers a sleek, drag-and-drop interface for data analytics with native integration to pull data from CSVs, JSON files, Google Sheets, SQL databases, and that back corner of the dryer where you’ve inevitably forgotten a sock. Data is automatically separated into dimensions (qualitative) and measures (quantitative) — and presumed to be ready for chart-making.
