Of course, if there are still a few data cleaning steps to be undertaken, Tableau can handle the dirty laundry as well. For example, it supports re-formatting data types and pivoting data from wide to tall format. When ready to make a chart, simply ctrl+click features of interest and an option from the “Show me” box of defaults. This simplicity of interaction enables even the most design-impaired data scientist to easily marshal data into a presentable format. Tableau will put your data into a suit and tie and send it to the boardroom. Follow these tips to go from “good” to “great” in your data visualization abilities. Gain inspiration from master chart-makers Throughout my time as a business analyst at a Big Four firm, these three blogs were my go-tos for how to create a great looking, functional Tableau dashboard. Keep these 4 guidelines in mind #1 — Sheets are the artist’s canvas and dashboards are the gallery wall. Sheets are for creating the artwork (ahem, charts), which you will then position onto a dashboard (using a tiled layout with containers — more on this in a second) along with any formatting elements. #2 — To save yourself time, set Default Properties for dimensions and measures. This will provide a unified approach to color, number of decimal points, sort order, etc. and prevent you from having to fiddle with these settings each time you go to use a given field. #3 — Along those lines, make use of the overarching Format Workbook and Format Dashboard options instead of one-off formatting tweaks. #4 — Avoid putting floating objects into your dashboards. Dragging charts around becomes a headache once you have more than two or three to work with. You can make your legends floating objects, but otherwise stay away from this “long-cut.” Instead, use the tiled layout, which forces objects to snap into place and automatically resizes if you change the size dimensions of your dashboard. Much faster and simpler in the long run. Get started with your first dashboard In summary, the Tableau platform is easier than finger paints to use, so if you’re ready to get started, Tableau Public is the free version that will allow you to create publicly accessible visualizations— like this one I put together after webscraping some info on questionable exempted developments from the Washing DC Office of Zoning — and share them to the cloud. Getting ready to present financials to the C-suite. Photo by Lisa Fotios on Pexels.
sampled: Rasheed Hooda published his first post on Medium on October 25, 2019, and exactly one year later, on October 24, 2020, he published his 400th story. That pace of output signals a serious commitment to showing up on the platform day after day, yet the financial return tells a different story. Over that full year, his total earnings from Medium came to $359.94, which averages just under 90 cents per story. He originally planned to evaluate the return on investment after the first six months of 2020. When that milestone arrived, he postponed the reckoning because he was genuinely enjoying the process of making friends and gaining followers. The community and the daily interactions felt rewarding enough to keep going, at least for a while longer. The numbers, however, remained stubbornly small. Publishing 400 posts in a year is a massive output, and earning $359.94 for that effort works out to a figure that is hard to frame as a sustainable income. The average of just under 90 cents per story means that each piece of writing, no matter how carefully crafted, contributed less than a dollar to his bottom line. In October 2020, something shifted. He received a sizable non-writing reward from the Universe, an opportunity that arrived outside the boundaries of the Medium platform. That event forced a hard look at where his energy was going and whether the writing life was the right container for his talents. He enjoys writing, but he does not feel passionate about it. His preferred communication modality is verbal, not written, which means the daily act of typing out posts was never a natural fit. The work was possible, and he did it consistently, but it never lit a fire that made him eager to sit down at the keyboard. He had previously enjoyed what he calls a Freedom Lifestyle by twisting balloons and giving them away, a simple and direct way of connecting with people. That path ended when 2020 turned out the way it did, and the forced stop left a gap that Medium writing partially filled. The balloon twisting was never about money, and the writing became a similar kind of outlet, though it lacked the same spark. A Turkish Proverb captures the logic of his decision: “Regardless of how far you’ve traveled down the wrong path, turn around.” After a full year and 400 posts, he decided to stop writing on Medium and explore a more fulfilling opportunity. The sunk cost of all those hours did not outweigh the clarity that arrived with the new reward. T. D. Jakes offered a framework that fits the moment: “If you can’t figure out your purpose, figure out your passion. For your passion will lead you right into your purpose.” Rasheed Hooda stepped away from the keyboard not because he failed, but because he recognized that his passion lives in a different kind of exchange, one that his year of writing helped him identify.

sampled: CAPTCHA stands for “completely automated public Turing test to tell computers and humans apart.” The test was designed to block bots by asking people to prove they are human through puzzles that machines could not solve. Improvements in artificial intelligence are making CAPTCHA challenges increasingly difficult for humans. As machine learning advances, the puzzles must become harder to stay ahead of automated scripts. Jason Polakis published a 2016 paper showing Google’s own tools could solve Google’s CAPTCHAs. His research at the University of Illinois at Chicago demonstrated that the very systems meant to stop bots were vulnerable to the company’s own technology. Machine learning now matches or exceeds human performance on basic text, image, and voice recognition. This shift means tasks once considered reliable proof of humanity no longer provide a secure barrier. CAPTCHA challenges discriminate against users with vision, hearing, or learning disabilities. A test that relies on seeing distorted text or hearing garbled audio immediately excludes people who cannot perceive those formats. Inclusive design requires content to be convertible into different formats, which CAPTCHAs prevent. A properly accessible website lets users transform information into modes they can process, but a visual puzzle blocks that conversion. Assistive technologies and bots use similar machine-learning AI, locking out disabled users. Screen readers and other tools rely on algorithms that overlap with bot capabilities, so sites often block both. The arms race between bots and CAPTCHAs is reaching a point where bots consistently beat humans. The puzzles have become so complex that legitimate users fail more often than the automated systems they are meant to stop. Jason Polakis described the situation clearly when he said, “Machine learning is now about as good as humans at basic text, image, and voice recognition tasks. We’re at a point where making it harder for software ends up making it too hard for many people. We need some alternative, but there’s not a concrete plan yet.” His warning highlights a growing tension between security and usability. The tools that once protected websites are now creating barriers that affect a fifth of the population with a disability. Google is developing reCAPTCHA v3, which analyzes broader user behavior instead of presenting challenges. The new approach monitors how people interact with a page to assign a risk score without interrupting the experience. Behavior-based bot detection may incorrectly flag disabled users who interact with websites differently. Someone who navigates with a keyboard only or uses a screen reader might generate patterns that look suspicious to the system. Robin Christopherson of AbilityNet has raised concerns about these unintended consequences. Writing for The Verge, he explained how well-intentioned security measures can systematically exclude people from digital services. The problem grows more urgent as everyday tasks move online. Banking, shopping, and government services all rely on bot detection that was not designed with diverse human interaction in mind. Stephen Hawking’s experience illustrated the gap between security assumptions and real-world use. A system that demands a mouse click or a visual puzzle fails the moment it encounters someone using alternative input methods. The search for a better solution continues without a clear roadmap. The current path leads toward tests that are either too easy for bots or too hard for the people they are supposed to protect.

original: The Neuroscience of Slowing Down to Accomplish More Rushing is a false economy Photo by Chinmay Singh from Pexels When I was little, my grandmother always told me, “Less haste, more speed.” I really didn’t get what she was trying to tell me. On first hearing it, I thought it was a contradiction to state that less going fast actually meant more going fast — I couldn’t wrap my head around the difference between haste and speed. But then I was the kind of kid that did everything at 100 miles per hour, and that was something I took into adulthood with me. In my first career in the hospitality industry, I was always rushing, and I was always super stressed. I had a team of staff underneath me, but I hated delegating, stuck in my belief that if you wanted something done right then you needed to do it yourself. I left that industry aged 29, exhausted and desperate for change in my life. I learned better When I decided on a career change and went to University, I studied Cognitive Neuroscience. I began to learn so much that explained who I was as a person, and why I had been so stressed and depleted in my first career. Knowing what I had been doing to my brain, I had to change my approach. Executive function is what separates us from the animals Our ‘executive functions’ are those more complex thought processes, like planning for the future and thinking in an abstract way. These executive functions separate us from the other mammals. When I was organizing the catering for big events, I was using a lot of planning and logistical thinking, and this was really quite tiring. Our working memory is a part of our executive functions, which are all associated with the prefrontal cortex. Working memory capacity As far as studies can tell, our working memory has a very finite capacity. It has long been understood that the average person can hold 7 items (problems or things to remember) in their working memory, with an average variation of -2 or +2. So to put that in simple terms; if you are trying to remember a few things to do later, while considering a couple of logistical issues, and then your phone rings and somebody needs you — your working memory is now maxed out and you can’t handle anything else. Why am I sharing this? Put simply, when your working memory is at full capacity, the effect on your cognition is similar to having too many browser tabs open on your laptop. Things start to slow down and your system becomes less efficient — maybe even overwhelmed. When we try to do too much at once, typically in a bid to save time, we end up depleting our reserves, slowing us down in the long run. We can sustain only very short bursts of this intense kind of working and thinking. If you’ve ever worked in the events industry then you will know the feeling of exhaustion after working a busy event. It’s almost like an ‘energy hangover’ for the next few days. But if you want to achieve more over a sustained period of time, then the science-backed advice is to keep things simple and not try to pack everything in at once. And if you need to be warned about the pitfalls of multi tasking, then check out this story on task switching and focus.
sampled: The Netflix docuseries High Score arrived as a six-part look at video game history, and I watched it with the same curiosity I bring to any deep archive of the medium. It sent me back to my own starting point, which was Duck Hunt on the original Nintendo Entertainment System, the first game I can remember playing. That memory sits inside a much longer timeline because I have owned almost every video game console released in the last three decades. The show made me realize how much my habits have shifted, since my gaming has slowed in recent years and I now often play titles three or four years after their release. Right now I am working through Shadow of the Tomb Raider, the third game in the rebooted series that reimagines Lara Croft for a modern audience. The reboot follows her trying to stop the secret society Trinity from destroying the world, a premise that promises globe-spanning adventure and ancient mysteries. I genuinely enjoy the exploration in Shadow of the Tomb Raider, from scaling overgrown ruins to discovering hidden chambers that reward patient observation. The problem is that I dislike the required killing, which interrupts the rhythm of discovery and forces me into extended gunfights I never asked for. The game insists that the only way to advance the story is to clear rooms full of armed enemies, and I find that limitation exhausting. I do not want to play any game where killing is the only way to advance the story, because it turns what could be a personal journey into a repetitive exercise in body counts. This frustration has been building for a while, and it recently pushed me back toward a very different kind of experience. I have been drawn back to No Man's Sky, a 2016 game focused on exploration, mining, and trading across a procedurally generated universe that feels genuinely endless. No Man's Sky provides open-ended choices, allowing players to avoid combat entirely if they prefer to chart planets, build bases, or simply drift through star systems in quiet solitude. That freedom is exactly what I need when a linear action game leaves me feeling like a reluctant mercenary. I keep thinking about how Lara Croft could be written to match the explorer she is supposed to be. I wish she could sneak past enemies instead of being forced into lethal combat, using her intelligence and athleticism to bypass threats rather than mow them down. The Tomb Raider series has always sold itself on discovery and ancient secrets, yet the reboot trilogy keeps locking progression behind mandatory shootouts. Every time I clear a wave of Trinity soldiers I feel less like an archaeologist and more like a soldier who happens to carry a climbing axe. Other games have proven that you can build tension and stakes without requiring the player to kill people. Horizon Zero Dawn is praised for its story and for featuring conflict against machines rather than people, which lets Aloy fight for survival without turning her into a mass murderer. That design choice respects the player's desire to engage with a world on their own terms, and it makes the narrative feel more thoughtful. When the enemies are mechanical creatures, every encounter can still be dangerous and spectacular without forcing the protagonist to take human lives. I keep returning to No Man's Sky because it trusts me to decide what kind of experience I want, whether that means peaceful cataloging or high-stakes resource runs. Games that offer that kind of agency remind me why I fell in love with the medium in the first place, back when a plastic light gun and a laughing dog were enough to make an afternoon feel limitless.

original: I’ve Learned to Receive Messages From The Universe The signs will be obvious to you if you just tune in Photo by Jen Theodore on Unsplash “One of your ancestors from Europe is watching over you,” said a woman to me when I was 19 years old, working at a chocolate store in Union Station in DC. She was buying a truffle from me, wearing a woven scarf, and looked at me with complete calm and sincerity. I was bewildered. I went home and called my grandmother, and she speculated about who in the family it could be. I felt strongly that it was someone from her father’s side. It was just a feeling. Since then, years later, I have now become very familiar with these ‘feelings’. When I have them, what used to seem like a hunch now seems like a complete certainty. I’ve learned to receive messages from my ‘third eye’, my intuition — the eye I have into the realm of knowledge that logic and science cannot explain. Anyone can receive messages from the universe. All you have to do is open yourself to it. The more you meditate, become aware, and tune into the energy around you, the more clear the messages will become. There are some things I’ve listed here to help you open yourself to the messages. Nothing is a Coincidence It’s hard to let go of the idea that the world you experience is dead, random, and meaningless. Growing up, this is what we learn. We live in a universe teeming with energies, and we take part in it, yet we deny this all the time. It interacts with us, and it is affected by our energy. Once you let go of the idea you were probably raised to believe — that ‘weird’ things that happen are coincidences — you’ll be ready to receive the messages that have probably been lost on you for your entire life. Have you heard a voice sometimes when you are the only one hearing it? Have you seen the future coming, but denied it because you think there’s no such thing as clairvoyance? Do you dismiss weird occurrences and instead, try to explain them logically? Most people block out their intuition because it doesn’t make sense in the world they are used to. Don’t be like them. Animals Carry Messages Early on, the messages I was used to receiving were always in the form of animals. I’ve come to view animals as spirits that are embodying qualities they want you to examine. If a bluebird lands on your shoulder and flies away, you are feeling freedom or about to take off. If you see a dead raccoon, then something clever and beautiful has died in you. All you have to do is look closely at what’s going on. Crows have always been very interesting to me. Their behavior can always be interpreted, and I often think it is an omen. Crows that surround you in the trees are definitely trying to make you aware of something. But they can also embody good energy.
sampled: My daughter arrived through an emergency C-section at 26 weeks, and she weighed only 2 pounds and 2 ounces. That moment began a chapter of my life I could never have prepared for, one that would test every idea I had about strength and fear. The pregnancy had already been a storm of uncertainty from the very beginning. At six weeks, my wife was told she had suffered a miscarriage, and we were sent home carrying a grief that felt absolute and final. A week after that devastating diagnosis, a doctor found a heartbeat during a follow-up visit. That same emergency room trip also revealed a tumor growing inside my wife, piling one impossible piece of news on top of another. The relief of the heartbeat was short-lived because at 20 weeks my wife’s water broke. We were told that holding the pregnancy for just four more weeks would give the baby a chance at viability, so we focused on nothing but getting through each day. A doctor sat me down and explained that babies in our daughter’s situation had a 1% chance of survival. I was alone when I heard those scenarios, which included the possible deaths of both my wife and my daughter, and the weight of that conversation has never fully left me. The emergency C-section at 26 weeks felt like the culmination of months of helpless waiting. When my daughter was born weighing 2 pounds and 2 ounces, I could not hold her for the first 8 days, and those days stretched into a strange, hollow eternity. She spent 149 days in the hospital before she finally came home. Those months were a blur of monitors, beeping machines, and the slow, fragile work of letting her grow strong enough to leave the sterile room she had always known. After her traumatic birth, I found myself wrestling with survivor’s guilt. I had walked out of the hospital with my life intact while my daughter fought for every breath, and that contrast settled into a quiet, persistent ache I did not know how to name. Survivor’s guilt is commonly seen among Holocaust survivors, war veterans, and disaster survivors. I learned that it can also take root in a NICU parent who watches a tiny body endure procedures and setbacks while he stands by, physically whole but emotionally fractured. I kept replaying the moment I was alone with the doctor, hearing those brutal percentages and the talk of losing them both. That memory became a loop I could not escape, even after my daughter’s monitors stopped beeping and we finally walked through our front door. My wife carried her own scars from the tumor discovery and the months of bed rest, and I watched her navigate recovery while I sorted through my guilt in silence. The 149 days in the hospital had ended, but the mental weight of those days lingered in our home. My daughter is here now, and her presence rewrites none of the terror but sits alongside it. The 1% chance, the 2-pound body, and the 8 days of waiting to hold her remain fixed points on a timeline that changed how I understand survival.

original: “Naked girl, covered in Napalm. Five marines Raising the Flag, Mount Suribachi. V for Victory. They remember the pictures. Fifty years from now, they’ll have forgotten the war.“ Wag the Dog (1997) A picture is worth a thousand words, and in politics there are a lot of words. From the early cave paintings in Bhimbetka (dated 13,000 BC to 12,700 BC) humans have used visual methods to describe their own version of events in order to shape public perception. Religion began to spread through the illiterate parts of the world, largely due to the strong iconography that came alongside it. In the 19th century royal families, great conquerors and heroic battles were commemorated in elaborate, gigantic paintings, which solidified the way we think about those events and people hundreds of years later. In the 20th century, politicians used Conscripted Art and propaganda to control public opinion. Thus, when we talk about design in politics, we’re not just thinking about a candidate’s great logo or a movement’s compelling website, we’re considering all the visual elements that project a certain image and message. Reaching the Global Village In the 21st century, the age of the internet and social media, we find ourselves in a reality where not having a clear, strong, and– most importantly, memorable– visual identity is not an option. We all live in a global village, and the one language almost all of us speak is the visual language. As a people, we like to think we’ve come a long way since the days of shameless political propaganda and that we are much more suave now. We won’t be fooled by posters and political infomercials that are trying to bluntly paint a different picture from what we know to be true. The good news is that we are much more sophisticated than that. The bad news is that so are the campaigners. Social media has contributed massively to the proliferation of design in politics. It’s not just that we focus so often on visual elements as we scroll through media-sharing platforms like Instagram, Twitter, and Facebook; it’s also about the sheer volume of content that is being produced and the rate at which it’s shared. To keep viewers’ interest, you need a graphic language, templates, and constant production. In that way, social media allows smaller movements or campaigns to gain recognition on the basis of their graphic design presence: it’s not just what you say, it’s also how you look. The Medium is the Message America, in many ways, is a perfect example of how the relationship between design and politics has evolved in the digital era. Many have called Barack Obama “the social media president,“ since he was the first holder of the office to effectively utilize the tools offered by the internet. “The high production value and disciplined branding of the Obama campaigns deserve a great deal of credit for raising the standards of campaign branding, proving that great branding provides a powerful platform to build trust, tell stories, and engage the public imagination,“ writes Deroy Peraza for fastcompany.com. The Obama campaigns have also showed us once more that Marshall Mcluhan was right when he said in 1964 that “The Medium is the Message“; it is certainly true when it comes to politics.
sampled: Vertical farming grows crops in vertically stacked layers without soil or natural light, shifting agriculture into controlled indoor environments. The approach moves production from sprawling countryside fields into dense city centers, cutting transport distances and land use. LEDs, sensors, and robots manage lighting, climate, and harvesting inside these facilities, replacing sun and rain with precise automation. This tight control lets growers fine-tune conditions for each plant variety without relying on weather or seasons. The concept draws on a long history of protected cultivation that stretches back to Roman times, when early indoor methods sheltered delicate plants. Centuries later, greenhouses became widespread in Europe during the 17th century and eventually helped the Netherlands become the world’s second largest food exporter. Dickson Despommier popularized vertical farming as a way to feed millions while reducing carbon emissions, deforestation, and chemical fertilizer use. His vision took shape after looking at New York City and imagining skyscrapers filled with food instead of offices. A vertical farm in Japan harvests lettuce within 40 days and produces 21,000 heads daily from two towers. Each tower covers 900 square meters, and the operation runs year-round without pesticides, delivering fresh greens straight to nearby markets. Vertical farming provides year-round fresh vegetables without pesticides and with short farm-to-plate distances. That means produce can reach consumers within hours of harvest, keeping nutrient loss low and flavor high. The two main water-based methods used in these systems are aeroponics and hydroponics, which suspend roots in air or nutrient solutions instead of dirt. Both approaches recycle water continuously, using a fraction of what open fields require. Sensors and cameras collect data to enable real-time decisions improving plant health, growth, and yield. Machine learning models process this information to adjust light spectra, humidity, and nutrient mixes automatically. Statista projects the vertical farming market to be worth USD 6.4 billion by 2023, reflecting rapid investment in the United States, Japan, and other early adopters. The figure signals growing confidence that indoor agriculture can scale beyond niche leafy greens. The UN FAO states food production must increase by 70 percent by 2050 to feed a projected 9.1 billion people. Traditional farming alone struggles to meet that target while coping with soil degradation, water scarcity, and climate volatility. One US vertical farm claims a yield increase of 350 times over open fields, along with water usage of just 1 percent compared to traditional techniques. Such numbers highlight the efficiency potential when every variable is optimized indoors. High initial investment and electricity costs challenge the business model, and renewable energy could improve environmental claims. Critics point out that powering LED arrays and climate systems can undercut the sustainability promise if grids rely on fossil fuels. Indoor farming has existed since Roman times, but the current wave integrates artificial intelligence in ways earlier growers never imagined. The fusion of robotics, data analytics, and plant science marks a distinct break from simple greenhouse production. The Japanese facility’s daily output of 21,000 lettuce heads shows how dense urban production can supplement rural supply chains. It also demonstrates that leafy greens thrive under artificial light, though staple crops like wheat and rice remain harder to grow profitably indoors. Vertical farming reduces environmental impact by moving production from countryside to cities, yet its long-term viability depends on cheaper clean energy and broader crop diversity. The race to refine those economics is now unfolding across labs and commercial farms worldwide.

original: One of the most interesting aspects of the Design Thinking process, is not only the strengthening of the relationships that are created within the Product Design team (including not only Designers, but an entire ecosystem where Developers, Product Owners, Customer Support Groups, Marketing Professionals, Inventory Managers, to name but a few, collaborate), but also of course with the Users/Clients, who become part of that product journey, not only uncovering the solution itself, but how that product eventually morphs and continues to live past launch/release cycles. Another rewarding aspect of the process itself has always been the imminent realization that whatever is uncovered, tested and refined, has to eventually be built, within a series of constraints. These constraints can be of multiple natures, be it financial, platform wise, resources, timelines, among others, all of which is going to be the focus of attention for this article. Constraints. Every Product Design initiative always has a series of constraints associated with it, something that should be clearly showcased when the process starts. Further constraints may be added to the scope of the initiative particularly as time goes on, but initially there’s already a listing of topics that all the participants in the Design Thinking process need to be aware of. Those general constraints are associated with a trifecta of factors: timelines, resources and finances. Expanding on these fundamentally operational constraints: timelines are part of the DNA of any project that is tackled. The need to release something to market, an MVP that is ultimately viable, which can be expanded upon, creates challenges from the Design process itself, in terms of running effective Research, Validation, Iterations, Testing exercises. All these phases provide different types of input into the solution that is being morphed, but once again Designers have to forcibly be strategic about how they devote time to each one of them (and how they bring different players to these phases, in order to gather the information they need to keep the process breezing along). Timelines are also deeply entwined with Resource allocation. Depending on the availability of team members, of different natures of course, allows for a lot of these processes and initiatives to be conducted more rapidly, and enable for iterative cycles for instance, to be produced in a speedier manner. Resource availability is also tied with different layers of expertise, not just from a Design perspective, but also from other professionals who are involved in the process, and need to be available to participate in it. That includes for instance, professionals in Product Ownership, Development, Customer Support, Marketing, Sales, Inventory Management, the list goes on, but summarily, they all have a pivotal impact in the solutioning effort, and their contribution should always be accounted for. Matter of factly: without enough resources, the challenges to fulfill & keep the timelines established can become a herculean task in itself. Deeply entwined with the previous two factors, there is of course the financial constraints that have implications across the board.
sampled: No-code tools have reshaped how founders build startups around a minimum viable product, offering a path that sidesteps the custom system headaches Joe Procopio endured when he launched his first company 20 years ago. Back then he had no choice but to construct a proprietary setup to track business data from scratch. Now a founder can assemble the same operational backbone in hours without writing a single line of code. A poll of entrepreneurs inside the Teaching Startup community revealed a telling gap. Almost half of the respondents admitted they only track sales, a practice Procopio likens to relying on sticky notes. That narrow focus leaves entire swaths of the business invisible. One well-financed startup he encountered was pulling in $6 million in monthly revenue yet burning $7 million every month because no one had wired cost tracking into the daily workflow. Every startup needs a single system of record for customers that follows them from the first prospect touchpoint all the way through churn. A spreadsheet can serve that purpose perfectly well as long as every customer gets a unique ID. The real danger is skipping the system entirely and operating on instinct. The discipline of a central customer record forces clarity. When a founder logs each interaction against that unique ID, patterns that were hidden inside email threads and memory start to surface. The spreadsheet becomes the startup’s operational memory, and it costs nothing to maintain. Early-stage teams should resist the temptation to build elaborate marketing dashboards before they have proven causation between spend and sales. Aggregate marketing data is enough at first. If a founder drops $100 on a digital ad campaign, the only question that matters is whether the customer system of record shows new prospects tied to that campaign. Granular channel metrics can wait until the link to revenue is solid. Sales data, by contrast, must be tied back to the customer record immediately and kept as real-time as the tools allow. The moment a payment clears in Stripe or a deal stage advances in a lightweight CRM, that change should land in the master spreadsheet. The no-code ecosystem makes those connections trivial. Zapier sits at the center of the operation, watching for events in Stripe, MailChimp, Quickbooks, Salesforce, or Hubspot and then updating the spreadsheet automatically. A new subscriber in MailChimp can trigger a row creation. A closed invoice in Quickbooks can flip a status field. Slack paired with Zapier adds a real-time notification layer so the whole team sees when a high-value customer moves or a churn risk spikes. The stack feels custom-built even though it is stitched together with off-the-shelf parts. These no-code pipelines are not meant to last forever. A startup that finds product-market fit will eventually outgrow the spreadsheet and the web of Zaps. The value of the no-code phase is that it forces the team to define exactly what data matters and how it relates. When the time comes to commission a custom system, the engineers will inherit a battle-tested data structure instead of a blank whiteboard. The temporary scaffolding becomes the permanent blueprint.

original: It’s not really about being able to build a fire or carry a heavy pack over long distances, it’s a general feeling of competence that imbues you with a sense of confidence. And that realization of “I can do this” can carry over into other parts of life. Having accomplished one hard task, you believe you can problem-solve and persevere through other difficult situations as well. Now faced with the challenge of a global pandemic, it seems that many of us are brushing up on our practical skills, although they’re more Little House on the Prairie than My Side of the Mountain. And while knitting a scarf may not directly relate to surviving a deadly virus, it does provide a feeling of competence and control. Maybe we can’t ensure that our parents will be safe or we won’t lose our jobs, but we can turn flour, water, and yeast into bread and grow our own sustenance from vegetable trimmings and seedlings. And in gaining control over that facet of our lives, we gain a little control over the rest of our lives, too. “A lot of this pandemic and the things surrounding it are out of our control,” Robinson says. “It’s not our personal choice to stay at home, it’s not our personal choice not to go into the office. Homemaking tasks give you that bit of control and a sense of accomplishment.” A concrete feeling of accomplishment is something that many of us were lacking even before the novel coronavirus emerged, says John Hudson, chief survival instructor for the British military. As our lives have become more virtual, outdoor survival courses and shows like Naked and Afraid have risen in popularity over the last decade. Hudson, who’s applied his survival knowledge to the current situation in the e-book How to Survive a Pandemic, thinks a big reason for this appeal is the instant gratification that living off the land offers people. When the only evidence that the sacrifices we’re making through social distancing are working is that nothing happens, it makes sense that so many of us would yearn for a more tangible outcome from our efforts. “We spend an enormous amount of our working hours indoors, looking at a screen, answering emails … and we never really see an immediate or even any tangible result of our efforts,” he says. “Doing survival instruction, there’s a definite reward in my world if you complete a task. It’s almost an immediate reward because you know if you’ve succeeded or failed [in building shelter or lighting a fire] straight away.” When so much in our lives is uncertain, and the only evidence that the sacrifices we’re making through social distancing are working is that nothing happens, it makes sense that so many of us would yearn for a more tangible outcome from our efforts. “It may be out of boredom, but when we’re so anxious and you can cook, that’s an effort-based reward,” says Kelly Lambert, PhD, a professor of behavioral neuroscience at the University of Richmond.
sampled: When Piero Borrelli set out to uncover the small influence tricks that make someone truly loved in the office, he discovered that the entire playbook rests on a single, surprisingly simple secret. His exploration draws heavily on Dale Carnegie’s timeless bestseller How to Win Friends and Influence People, a book that has shaped workplace relationships for decades. The foundational principle, as Carnegie himself put it, is this: “You can make more friends in two months by becoming interested in other people than you can in two years by trying to get other people interested in you.” Borrelli, who works as a software engineer in the tech field, learned this lesson firsthand when he decided to approach a coworker with sincere curiosity about her design work. He asked thoughtful questions and listened carefully, not to steer the conversation toward his own projects, but to understand her craft and the principles that guided her decisions. That genuine engagement transformed a routine office interaction into something far more meaningful. The coworker noticed the depth of his interest and responded with an openness that surprised him, offering ongoing support and a standing invitation to seek her guidance whenever he needed it. Her reaction was immediate and warm. She told him, “I feel like you really like this, and I’m happy you listen with so much passion. Feel free to come back to me and ask me anything whenever your need it.” Those words confirmed for Borrelli that showing authentic interest creates a bridge that no amount of self-promotion can build. The experience with the designer was not an isolated experiment. Borrelli began applying the same interest-driven approach with people from every corner of the company, from sales to accounting to operations. He found that when he set aside his own agenda and focused entirely on what others could teach him, the barriers between departments started to dissolve. Colleagues who might have remained distant became collaborators, and the office felt less like a collection of silos and more like a network of willing teachers. Salespeople taught Borrelli influence techniques that no engineering textbook ever covered, showing him how to read a room and communicate value in ways that felt natural rather than manipulative. Accounting helped Borrelli understand how a company works at the structural level, revealing the financial rhythms and constraints that shaped decisions far beyond his own team. Those conversations gave him a broader view of the business, one that made his technical work more relevant and his contributions more visible. The pattern repeated itself across every interaction: the more he learned about others, the more they wanted to help him succeed. Being interested in others leads to knowledge, networking, and human bonding in ways that transactional office politics never can. Ralph Waldo Emerson once observed that people carry their own weather, and Borrelli’s approach proves that the climate of a workplace changes when curiosity replaces self-interest. By treating every colleague as a source of insight, he built a reputation not as someone who merely wanted to get ahead, but as someone who genuinely valued the people around him. That shift, he insists, is the real influence trick, and it costs nothing but attention.

original: NEWSLETTER The CRISPR Nobel Prize & Data Stored in DNA Gets Destroyed This Week in Synthetic Biology (Issue #11) Receive this newsletter every Friday morning! Sign up here: https://synbio.substack.com/ Data, Stored in DNA, Gets Destroyed (But In A Good Way) DNA is promising for data storage, mainly because a single gram of DNA can store 256 petabytes of information. But there’s a problem: DNA is, in some cases, too stable. To remove a user’s data from DNA on “nucleic acid hard drives” of the future, scientists first need to develop better ways to selectively target, and destroy, DNA. A new method, published in Nature Communications, could be a contender for wiping DNA hard drives in the year 2087 (assuming the human race survives that long). DNA sequences, each containing a “True” barcode and one, or several, “False” barcodes, are first mixed together. Then, “truth markers” — DNA sequences that selectively bind to the “True” sequences — are added to the mixture. If the mixture is then heated to 95 degrees Celsius, the “truth markers” fall off and information from the “True” bits is lost. It’s a simple technique, with promising results. The researchers showed that “8 separate bitmap images can be stably encoded and read after storage at 25 °C for 65 days with an average of over 99% correct information recall, which extrapolates to a half-life of over 15 years at 25 °C. Heating to 95 °C for 5 minutes, however, permanently erases the message.” An enzymatic pathway has been assembled on top of a Tobacco mosaic virus. Using peptide “linkers”, the scientists, based in Hong Kong, tethered “three terpene biosynthetic enzymes” to the outer particles of the virus, and grew them inside of E. coli cells. The goal was to explore how the proximity of enzymes impacts the bioproduction of a molecule (in this case, amorpha-4,11-diene). Since the Tobacco mosaic virus is 300nm long, metabolic engineers could presumably use it as a foundation to assemble any number of complex enzymatic pathways. This study was published in Bioconjugate Chemistry. Deep Learning to Design RNA “Switches” Two studies, published in Nature Communications, used deep learning to guide the engineering of RNA “toehold switches”. These RNA switches are, basically, synthetic RNA sequences that can be turned ON and OFF. In their OFF state, the toehold switches form a hairpin loop and cannot be read by the ribosomes — they do not produce a protein. The addition of an RNA “trigger”, however, can be used to turn a toehold switch ON; translation can proceed. Toehold switches are especially useful because a lot of them can be present in a cell at the same time, and triggers can be designed for each of them. This means that many genes can be precisely controlled for synthetic biology applications. Unfortunately, toehold switches are really difficult to design, and even a slight tweak to a sequence can impact their utility. In the first study, led by Nicolaas M. Angenent-Mari, over 90,000 toehold switches were synthesized and tested using clever experiments that enabled the activity of each toehold switch to be individually assessed. After testing each of the RNAs, data was fed into a deep learning model (which I won’t even pretend to understand). The output from that model looks promising: “[Deep Neural Networks] trained on nucleotide sequences outperform (R2 = 0.43–0.70) previous state-of-the-art thermodynamic and kinetic models (R2 = 0.04–0.15).” In the second study, led by Jacqueline Valeri, two “deep learning architectures” were introduced — called STORM and NuSpeak — to improve the performance of RNA toehold switches. Both studies are open access, and represent a paradigm shift in how quickly synthetic biologists will be able to design and engineer biological molecules that behave as expected. The vast majority of plants on earth are C3 plants; when it’s hot or dry, C3 plants close their stomas, oxygen builds up, and the efficiency of photosynthesis goes down.
sampled: Decision fatigue is real. Your brain gets tired just like your muscles do after a long workout. A Columbia University study tracked 1,112 parole trials over 10 months. Researchers found something unsettling about how judges made life-altering rulings. The outcomes had little to do with the crime and everything to do with the clock. Every choice you make slowly drains a finite tank of mental energy. When that tank runs low the brain starts conserving resources by defaulting to the path of least resistance. In a courtroom that means denying parole because saying no is the easier, safer option. The study proved that the time of day mattered more than the severity of the offense or the prisoner’s background. At the very start of the morning session criminals had up to a 65 percent chance of receiving a favorable judgment. Judges who were rested and mentally refreshed evaluated each case with nuance and care. They weighed evidence, considered rehabilitation, and granted parole at a steady clip. That careful deliberation burned through their cognitive reserves hour by hour. The favorable judgment odds dropped to near zero before the first break. As the morning wore on the rate of parole grants collapsed toward zero because the judges were experiencing deep decision fatigue. Their brains were so depleted that the safest default was to simply maintain the status quo and keep the prisoner incarcerated. The pattern reversed sharply after a lunch break restored some mental energy. Suddenly the odds of parole jumped back up again only to begin their slow decline toward zero by the end of the afternoon session. The 1,100 cases covered a wide range of crimes including rape, robbery, and embezzlement. The trend held steady across every category which made the finding even more disturbing. The timing effect was not subtle. It was the single biggest predictor of whether someone would walk free or stay behind bars. The study stripped away any illusion that these were purely rational legal decisions. Instead the judges were operating on a dwindling cognitive battery that recharged only after food and rest. Mental fatigue does not announce itself with a yawn or a heavy eyelid. It quietly shifts your decision strategy from careful analysis to automatic shortcuts. You stop distinguishing between options and start picking whatever feels easiest in the moment. This is not a character flaw or a sign of weakness. The brain’s executive function relies on glucose and neural resources that get burned up with every choice no matter how small. When the supply runs low the quality of your decisions plummets. The Columbia University research revealed that even highly trained professionals with decades of experience are not immune. The judges believed they were ruling on the merits of each case but their brains were being hijacked by a biological limit they could not feel. You face the same invisible drain every day. The cumulative effect of choosing what to wear, what to eat, which email to answer first, and how to respond to a tense message all chip away at the same reserve. By late afternoon you are running on empty and your brain starts protecting itself by avoiding complex decisions altogether. The parole study offers a stark warning about trusting your gut when you are tired. Those judges were not lazy or indifferent. They were simply human. The fix is not to try harder or push through the fog. The only reliable way to protect decision quality is to structure your day around the brain’s natural rhythm. Tackle the most consequential choices early in the morning when your mental energy peaks. Schedule breaks that genuinely disconnect you from decision-making so your cognitive reserves can partially recharge. Batch low-stakes choices together and handle them in a single block rather than sprinkling them throughout the day. The goal is to spend your limited cognitive budget on the decisions that actually matter and stop pretending you have an infinite supply.

original: Meaning Eventually Finds Its Place In FKA Twigs’ Grandiose Artistic Vision Her latest LP “MAGDALENE” is an interstellar voyage through the dust of the broken heart to the planet of self During her long-lasting hiatus, the avant-garde pop princess FKA Twigs got crushed by the brutal hands of her troubled relationships — falling in love with the ex-blood sucker Robert Pattinson and splitting with him in a seemingly heart-wrecking manner. Two years following the end of this romance, twigs comes back feeling quite herself and ready to baptise her loyal fanbase in the career-defining shrift. In the pre-“MAGDALENE” era, British-born singer and songwriter Taliah Barnett took on a cunning challenge to manufacture the new RnB sound — blending her fragile-sounding soprano and the spooky art-house opera inspired imagery with the precision and inanimation of electronic music. Her efforts were met with universal critical acclaim, but looking in retrospect, the alien world twigs built around herself felt overwhelmed by her pompous visionary yet lacking raw human experience. In this sense, “MAGDALENE” comes through as a true revelation, being an album that runs on the fuel of imaginative lyricism and storytelling. Here, Twigs tries on the image of Mary Magdalene and tells us the love story with her very own Jesus, drawing inspiration from the chants of classical religious music and futuristic electronic sounds. The album starts with “thousand eyes” and, in an instance, enswathes you with a death-bearing sound of acapella choral signing and thud but heavy background instrumental, serving as a reminder of memorial liturgy music stripped off to its most naked condition. Alongside this soul-shivering melody, Twigs begins her Skaespherean story of spiritual death and thorny resurrection. If I walk out the door, it starts our last goodbye If you don’t pull me back, it wakes a thousand eyes Going forward, the narrative unfurls in a surprisingly cohesive manner, letting Twigs’ vocal arrangements and poetic talent shine the way they’ve never had before. No matter what it is — the antithesis of distorted chest voice and paper-light head voice on “home with you”, or the intimate insight into the secrets of womanhood on “mary magdalene” — Twigs serves us a bowl full of ripe-fruit she religiously gathered at the garden of Eden. There are many great moments on “MAGDALEN” — either lyrically, sonically or vocally — but the times it ascends to the sky-high levels lie at the intersection of the experimental search Twigs underwent in her previous work and the lucidity of pop-sound she tamed with the help of her fellow co-writers and co-producers. The result of this artistic confluence materialized in “sad day”, which might be remembered as one of the best pop tracks of this decade. Channelling Kate Bush ethereal timbre, Twigs starts the track by whispering simple yet beautiful lyrics into the isolation of her listener's auricles, and then the melody expands into this epic dance/electronic ballad where Skrillex’s production touch suddenly falls in place and electrifies the record. Bearing in mind how great the rest of the album is, it’s at best puzzling how “holy terrain” featuring Future made it to the final cut. It’s a commercially-baked, mediocre RnB song made to, perhaps, please the wider audience. A sad but not criminal oversight which gets forgotten as soon as the record ends. Despite being listed as the sixth track, “fallen alien” comes through as the culminating phase of the narrative. It’s the most experimental track on the album exposing Twigs in her most desperate state. She basically goes on a full-scale jihad against her former lover. Her vocals here are nothing less than transcending: incisive, hysterical, in a good sense of this word, and on the edge of breaking loose into a wild scream. The last three songs reveal Twigs meditating on the aftermath of relationships and reconciling with the damage left after it.
sampled: Andy Raskin met Christoph outside the Just for You Cafe in San Francisco. Christoph said, “I restructured our sales pitch using your Greatest Sales Deck framework and the results have been awesome. I’ve used it with a few prospects, and they engage at a deeper level, they get what we’re about faster, and they’re all moving to next steps.” The early-stage tech company CEO described a pattern that emerged almost immediately after he rebuilt the deck around a narrative arc instead of a feature dump. Prospects who had previously nodded politely through demos began asking sharper questions and volunteering their own challenges before Christoph even reached the solution slides. The shift in engagement felt so pronounced that he tracked it across every conversation that week. Christoph’s enthusiasm carried a quiet confidence that only deepened when he mentioned how the new flow changed the rhythm of his meetings. He no longer had to push through a list of capabilities while watching eyes glaze over. Instead the story pulled people into a shared understanding of why their current approach was breaking down and what a different future could look like. He paused after describing the momentum and added, “Well, it’s my VP of sales. He won’t even look at the new deck. Says he already has a deck, and that buyers don’t have time for a story, they just want to know how we solve their problem.” The VP’s objection was not unusual. Salespeople often push back on new decks because they inhibit discovery, replacing the organic back-and-forth of a conversation with a rigid slide sequence that feels like a performance. The tension Christoph faced is common inside growing companies. Sales leaders who have closed deals with a familiar deck rarely welcome a rewrite. The VP’s stance rested on a conviction that buyers are impatient and pragmatic, but that conviction ignored what Christoph had just witnessed in the field. Prospects who heard the story asked more thoughtful questions and moved to next steps faster than those who received the old product-centric walkthrough. The data from Christoph’s own pipeline contradicted the idea that storytelling slows things down. SpotMe, a company headquartered in Switzerland, uses “change in the world” slides to get prospects talking before the product even enters the conversation. Those slides frame a shift that makes the old way of doing things feel untenable, and they invite the buyer to describe how that shift is showing up inside their own organization. SpotMe’s customers see events as episodes in a greater journey, not self-contained shindigs, and that reframing changes the entire sales dialogue. When a prospect recognizes their own experience inside a story about change, they stop evaluating features and start imagining outcomes. The VP’s resistance was not about the deck’s effectiveness. It was about control. A narrative deck transfers some of that control to the buyer, who gets to co-author the conversation instead of receiving a monologue. For a sales leader who built a career on mastering the monologue, that can feel like a loss of leverage. Christoph understood the irony. His VP argued that buyers just want to know how the problem is solved, yet the new deck was producing exactly the kind of engaged, fast-moving buyers the VP claimed to want. The evidence was sitting in Christoph’s pipeline, but the VP refused to look at the deck that generated it. The standoff reflected a deeper split in how sales organizations think about time. One side sees a story as a luxury that busy buyers will reject. The other side sees a story as the shortest path to trust, because it mirrors how buyers actually make decisions. Christoph restructured his sales pitch using the Greatest Sales Deck framework, and the results spoke for themselves. The VP’s refusal to engage with the new deck did not erase those results. It just meant Christoph had to lead the change alone for a while longer.

sampled: Angela Friedman has lived through more than most people can imagine. She is 102. The New York resident has now survived Covid-19 twice, a feat that defies the odds at her advanced age. Her story begins long before the current pandemic. Her first encounter with the virus came in March 2020 while she was hospitalized for a minor procedure. That diagnosis was a frightening moment, but after a week in the hospital she was discharged and self-isolated until she recovered fully. It was a quiet, determined recovery that set the stage for what would come later. The second challenge arrived in late October 2020 when the nursing home where she lives contacted her daughter Joanne Merola. They reported that Angela had tested positive again and was showing symptoms. The news was a heavy blow for a family that had already navigated one bout with the disease. Her age made the situation even more alarming. She is 102. She was a baby during the 1918 flu pandemic. On 17 November 2020 she tested negative after isolation and treatment.

original: Today Google finally released the long awaited AI powered messaging app Allo. This messaging app is powered by the amazing Google AI which is a competitor of Apple’s Siri, Where Allo is prmarily text based and Siri is voice based. This app will also be competing with various other AI powered messaging apps such as the indian app Hike, China’s WeChat, Facebook’s M. So being that much of a geek and nerd to know all of the above like the back of my hand, I had to have this app ASAP so as soon as me and my friends heard the news and the app went live on the Play Store in India we all had it. We right away started testing out all the bells and whistles of the app, and one thing we all agreed on was damn the AI is good, because within 30 minutes of conversation in Hinglish (Hindi written with English Alphabets) between us and the AI had started predicting some of the basic stuff. And Damn we were impressed by that, because since forever we have been convinced that Hindi/Hinglish is a tough language to understand for an AI or a machine because of our experience with the AutoCorrect. The number of errors made by AutoCorrect in the US is not even close to the number it makes in India, and because of this we always end up either disabling it or set it to such a light mode that its nonexistent. So for an AI to start predicting words for to say in Hinglish such as “KYA?” correctly we were impressed. So we then started exploring more features, and we started playing with the google AI. We asked all the silly questions, all the good questions, all the funny questions and the AI never disappointed us. But during all this experimentation I realized something, the AI was predicting everything from what to say next to searching stuff that we wanted to discuss and stuff like that. For example I wanted to discuss about the girl in the movie Step Up, but obviously I did not remember her name, so my friend simply asked “@google Step Up 2 cast” and bam! google returned with the search results of this query. sampled: My experience with a previously diagnosed depressive episode gave me a reference point for identifying shifts in my mood. This prior knowledge was crucial because it allowed me to recognize the familiar signs of a returning depression. Using my Fitbit, I began to monitor the physical manifestations of my mental state, connecting the data to my feelings. My Fitbit statistics from one week in 2019 revealed a concerning combination of physical changes: I was losing weight, my workouts were unusually intense, my sleep was poor, and my resting heart rate had dropped significantly. This period was marked by prolonged, frequent crying spells that would occur daily and last for hours on end. A previous episode had involved crying every day for four months, with sessions initially lasting five to six hours before eventually reducing to one or two hours. During this more recent experience, I sometimes found myself waking up at 4 AM already crying, a stark indicator of the distress I was experiencing. These symptoms were all signs of a highly functioning depression. This form of depression can be particularly insidious and difficult for others to spot. It presents a facade of capability that masks the internal struggle. The internal experience was one of increased irritability and pervasive anxiety, creating a constant sense of being on edge. I felt hyper vigilant, as if my body was perpetually stuck in a "fight or flight" state, ready for a threat that never materialized. This state was exhausting. My capacity to reflect before reacting was severely diminished, which often led to impulsive actions and decisions. My ability to engage with and empathize with other people was also noticeably reduced, creating a sense of isolation. The effort required for social interaction felt insurmountable, further deepening my withdrawal from the world around me. The impact on my productivity was significant, as I found myself able to work for less than four hours each day. My cognitive functions were impaired. This decline in productivity created a backlog of commitments, including a staggering number of draft blog posts that needed completion. I had forty drafts from that one week alone that required attention. The pressure to keep up with my professional obligations clashed with my diminished capacity to perform. In early September 2019, the reality of my condition forced me to make difficult choices about my commitments. I had to cancel appointments and change plans that had been made during a healthier, more optimistic period of my life. This was a difficult but necessary step. To cope with the overwhelming emotional and psychological distress, I shifted my energy toward intense physical activities. I found a temporary release in pushing my body through running, cycling, and swimming. These intense workouts became a primary coping mechanism, a way to channel the turmoil I felt inside into physical exertion. This shift explained the unusual data my Fitbit was recording. The device was tracking both the symptoms and my attempts to manage them. During one week, my resting heart rate dropped significantly, a physiological marker captured by the device I wore daily. This data provided concrete evidence. This experience demonstrated how depression manifests physically. It affects sleep and heart rate. It changes how you move and work.

original: Use The 5/5/5 Rule To Unlock Your Focus And Build Up Discipline Four powerful questions to help you improve your life Photo by Jonathan Borba on Unsplash Feeling stuck? Maybe lacking focus? Need some more discipline in your life? I can help you out with that. And it won’t take much time at all either. Here’s how we can do it: perspective. Perspective is very powerful. It’s probably one of the most powerful things you can ever give yourself. It’s why you hire a coach or get a mentor to help you grow. They give you perspective that you cannot find on your own. Honestly, it’s even why many people hire a counselor too. That and sometimes we don’t trust ourselves fully. So, what if you could unlock a new perspective just with a few simple questions? The good news is you can. Allow me to share with you something I call the 5/5/5 Rule. It’s simple but also extremely powerful. Enter The Shockingly Simple 5/5/5 Rule I almost hesitate to call this a rule, but it really works. Just like the “Golden Rule.” It’s a good guide that you can just apply and use to get some results. So, without further ado, the 5/5/5 Rule is based on these 3 simple questions: How will you feel about something 5 minutes from now? How will you feel about something 5 months from now? How will you feel about something 5 years from now? You can apply these questions to pretty much anything. I’m going to use myself as example here, but I have a feeling I’m not alone with these struggles. Before we start, a disclaimer of sorts: you have to be totally honest with yourself. No sugarcoating, no half-truths. You must really be willing to dig deep and even dive back into your past in order to have the answer that you need in order to move forward. Okay, back to our regularly scheduled programming. Let’s look at a few examples of the 5/5/5 Rule in action. 4 Examples Of The 5/5/5 Rule In Action For example, you could ask… how will you feel 5 minutes from now if you eat that Oreo pie? Personally, I know I’ll feel like a bear that got shot with a tranquilizer dart (or two.) Let’s just say you won’t want to around me. The only options are to eat more of the pie or to immediately take a nap. So, the first question of the 5/5/5 Rule clearly tells me it’s best to not eat any of the Oreo pie. If I slip up and eat one piece, I know that I need to stop myself there, or I’m likely going to want more of the pie. The pattern has been established. I often rationalize and say, “It’s a special occasion,” or “It’s a small piece.” But those are just excuses that enable me to eat more than I should. Yes, I’m an Oreo pie addict of sorts. Some sweets just make me want more. If you struggle with sweets too, maybe you need to answer these same questions as well. How will you feel if you go on Facebook 5 minutes from now? I don’t know about you, but I’ll probably be distracted, annoyed, or envious. Anytime I have a very positive experience on Facebook it’s almost always on Messenger, connecting with a human being directly. That tells me it would be a much better idea to text or call a friend directly (or just use messenger) instead of going on Facebook.

sampled: Mid-life burnout describes chronic stress that can apply to your life in general, not just work. Burnout can be difficult to spot because it develops slowly over time. Its symptoms are also similar to those found in cases of mild-to-moderate depression, which can make identification challenging. One of the key signs of mid-life burnout is a feeling of physical and mental exhaustion. Another sign is cynicism about your relationships and your work. People may also develop a feeling of being ineffective in their daily lives. These factors combine to create a significant sense of being overwhelmed and depleted. It can be hard to spot. People experiencing this condition might feel professionally stuck, as if their career has stalled or is no longer fulfilling. They may also experience an increase in conflict with their partners, a sign that the stress is spilling over into personal relationships. Mid-life is a common time for burnout to appear for a variety of reasons. Many people in this stage of life are often raising children while simultaneously caring for elderly parents. These demanding family responsibilities are frequently juggled alongside the pressures of advancing their careers. This combination of stressors from multiple directions creates a perfect storm for developing chronic stress and eventual burnout. This is a common time. Physical symptoms can also manifest, including erratic sleep patterns that leave you feeling unrested. You might also experience stomach problems or frequent headaches. Unexplained pains can also be a physical indicator of this condition. These symptoms show how mental and emotional stress can impact the body directly. Burnout can develop slowly. A recommended strategy for dealing with burnout is to take a deliberate break from your routine. Setting clear boundaries around the demands placed on your time is also a crucial step. Another effective strategy is to conduct a thorough review of your current schedule and daily commitments. The goal is to identify nonessential activities. Once identified, you should work to eliminate these unnecessary commitments from your life. This can help you. Carving out regular time for yourself is a suggested method for combating the effects of burnout. It is important that some of this time is spent completely alone, providing space for reflection. This practice can help you reconnect with your own needs and desires away from external pressures. Making this a consistent habit is key to its effectiveness in restoring your mental and emotional balance. Finding something that creates a genuine sense of excitement is proposed as a way to reintroduce positive emotion. This strategy is focused on actively seeking out activities or interests that can spark joy and enthusiasm. Finding a source of excitement can help shift your focus away from the sources of stress and towards something that brings you a sense of purpose and pleasure, acting as a powerful counteragent to feelings of cynicism and ineffectiveness. Reviewing your schedule and eliminating unnecessary commitments is one important step you can take. Taking a break and setting boundaries around demands on your time is also a useful strategy. Carving out regular time for yourself is another suggested approach. Finding something that creates excitement is proposed as a way to reintroduce positive emotion into your life. Entrepreneur Tim Ferris has stated, "Excitement is the more practical synonym for happiness, and it is precisely what you should strive to chase. It is the cure-all."

original: If you want to design places catered for humans, placemaking is the concept you want to utilize. It’s UX on an urban scale. We plan, design, and develop according to the user’s needs and preferences, to ensure that the output is actually useful and usable for them. In this case, the user is the community — the people. In their book How to Turn a Place Around, Project for Public Spaces (PPS) proposes 11 principles to help urban planners, designers, and developers make places people actually want to live in. Let’s dissect them one by one. 1. The Community Is the Expert To begin a placemaking process, it’s best to first identify the talents and assets of the community. In every community, there are “experts” who can present valuable perspectives and insights about the area’s history, culture, functionalities, or any other aspect that’s considered meaningful for the people. By placing the community as the expert, it will foster a sense of “community ownership” which elevates the place’s importance in the eyes of its residents. 2. Create a Place, Not a Design When we hear “design,” our minds are likely to conjure images of shapes, colors, and other physical elements. However, it actually extends beyond that. As we understand from UX, design is about experience. In placemaking, every element (physical or otherwise), must serve a purpose. Mainly, the place should make people feel welcome and comfortable. This often translates to the development of effective relationships between the place, the people, and the activities. The goal here is to make the whole greater than the sum of its parts. 3. Look for Partners In a placemaking project, it’s best to look for partners as early as possible. These partners may come from the residents, local governments, educational institutions, museums, libraries, or other related organizations. Since placemaking is community-driven, and the place itself is supposed to foster community ownership, more partners will generally mean a greater sense of community. 4. You Can See a Lot Just by Observing Instead of guessing what might work or not work, it’s much more preferable to learn through observation. Simply by looking at how people are conducting their activities in a place, which elements they use or don’t use, what features they like, or don’t like; we can accurately identify what elements are missing and thus can be incorporated through placemaking. It’s also important to remember that the people’s preferences will evolve over time, and needs to be managed continuously. 5. Have a Vision A good placemaking approach shouldn’t just flow by “whatever seems easiest” or “whatever seems good at the time” — it should have a vision. This vision might include the physical shape of the place, its brand/image, the kinds of activities that might happen there, and so on. Ideally, the vision should come from the community itself. 6. Start with the Petunias: Lighter, Quicker, Cheaper Places are complex entities, and the placemaking practitioners shouldn’t expect to do everything correctly from the get-go. The best places are made through incremental improvements that are tested and refined over many years. For example, physical elements like seating, footpaths, or public artworks can be added and subtracted as needed, in time. Your first step can be as simple as planting a row of petunias. From there, you can gradually experiment with more intricate elements. 7.
sampled: Streamlit is a powerful library that provides users with the ability to deploy functional code directly from a simple Python script. This makes it an incredibly efficient tool for data scientists and machine learning researchers who need to share their work and create minimum viable products without extensive web development knowledge. The library stands out when compared to other frameworks, and the article positions Streamlit as a highly efficient option for deploying models to teams or clients. For solutions that require more advanced features or customization, the author suggests that a more robust framework like Flask is likely a better and more suitable choice. Competitors in this space include other well-known libraries such as Bokeh and Dash, each offering different approaches to data visualization and application deployment. While these alternatives exist, Streamlit has gained significant traction and recently secured a notable funding round, having raised $6 million to further its development and reach. Jupyter Notebooks are often used for research and report writing, but they are considered less practical when the goal is to share usable and interactive code with others. Streamlit fills this gap by allowing for a more seamless transition from a script to a shareable web application that others can interact with directly. Creating a simple web application is remarkably straightforward with this tool, demonstrating its core value proposition of simplicity and speed. A basic app featuring a dropdown menu and a corresponding line chart can be constructed with approximately 11 lines of Python code. This level of conciseness is a significant advantage over more traditional web development frameworks where a similar outcome would be far more involved. The author notes that building an equivalent application in a framework like Flask would necessitate writing hundreds of lines of code, covering routing, HTML templates, and backend logic. The example application demonstrates how to generate a simple interface for exploring different data distributions, a common task in data science. The user can select from a dropdown menu that offers two distribution choices, allowing for immediate visualization and comparison without complex setup. This sample application generates a random sample of 1000 data points to plot on the chart, providing a tangible example of how data can be manipulated and displayed. The code required for this is minimal, highlighting how Streamlit abstracts away the complexities of web development. A sample script, which could be saved as a file named "test.py," contains all the necessary logic to produce this interactive application. This single file encapsulates the user interface components, the data generation, and the plotting logic, making it easy to manage and share. Executing the application is just as simple as writing it, requiring only a single command to get started. By running the command "streamlit run test.py" in the terminal, the user can launch the entire web application locally on their machine. Once the command is executed, Streamlit automatically starts a local web server to host the newly created application for immediate use. This server makes the application accessible through a web browser, turning the Python script into a fully interactive tool. The local web server runs on a specific port, and the application can be viewed by navigating to the address http://localhost:8501/ in a browser. This immediate feedback loop allows developers to see their changes in real time, greatly speeding up the development and iteration process for data-driven applications.
