original: For a founder, shutting down a company is like dumping your most beloved person in the entire world; even worse, finding them dead the next day. Failure is a common term for any rising startup. This never ceases to be true even with the overwhelming success stories repeatedly saturating our Quora feed. If anything, the percentage of startups failing in their first year continue to spring up through the last decade. It takes a gallant to be an entrepreneur, as nobody ever built any great company overnight. One has to be courageous enough to say yes when everyone else says no, ignoring statistics others lived by their entire lives. Like all founders, I suffered several terrible blows, got back up, and tried all over again in my quest to building a company. Mine might not be the journey with a pleasant ending, but then I owe my growth to it. I’d continue to regard entrepreneurship as a word on people’s Twitter bio if not for my attempt to pursue the not-so-pretty-adventure of building a company. What happened? It’s been a year since I had to make the bitter decision to shut down my company. It was a marketing consultancy I co-founded with a friend and worked with a team of a few people. We had a good run. Seven months later, we had to close everything down and let go of a startup we all grew so attached to. It was devastating. Looking back at the fuzzy memories now, I cherish how brave it was of me to undertake on such a journey with so little chance of scaling up, to begin with. I also came to see how wrong I was in the numerous assumptions I made while starting. I’ve seen how fundraising takes time — postponed meetings with potential investors drove me mad. It was frustrating, especially taking into account that my most important role as the CEO was to make sure that the company always has the necessary money to run it. Every other startup founder I’ve met told me a similar story, but I’ve never seen it clearer. I’ve also seen how vital it is to have a partner whose strengths complement my weaknesses, even if that means laying my best friend off the ride. Clinging to friends, at the expense of competence, is usually the first mistake many founders make in crashing their company. I’ve come to learn how building a product for a customer is underexplained. Your product can be perfect for the customer that is, unfortunately, in the wrong audience you’re marketing to. This factor aids in the failure of my company. We were so obsessed with offering the best service (our product) that we lost sight of who our ideal customers were. It was like taking a cruise, partying too much on the ship, only to wake up and find ourselves in the wilderness of the sea.
sampled: Brad Stollery published an article on 2018-07-06 that treats soccer penalties as more than a World Cup spectacle. The piece compares penalty-taking with decision-making lessons from poker, using a tense sporting moment to look at how people choose under pressure. Penalty shootouts are framed as a World Cup knockout-stage tiebreaker, where one kick can mean advancement or elimination. From there, the article turns a familiar soccer scene into a study of risk, fear, and judgment. A penalty kick is taken from twelve yards with only the goalkeeper to beat, so from the outside it can look straightforward. The article notes that penalties are scored about 3 in 4 times on average, which still leaves plenty of room for very public failure. The Economist studied World Cup penalties across a forty-year period, giving the article a statistical base for its argument. That analysis found that high shots succeeded more often than low shots overall, even though aiming high brought a different kind of risk. The numbers sharpen the point about where players choose to aim. Penalties aimed halfway up the goal or higher were saved 3% of the time, while 18% of high penalties missed the target and 5% of low penalties missed the target. The article states that high shots had a 79% success rate, compared with 72% for low shots. That comparison supports the idea that the better choice may also be the one that looks worse when it goes wrong. The piece argues that players often aim low because missing the target feels more humiliating than having a shot saved. A low attempt may be less effective in the data, but it can feel safer for the player’s image. Ego bias is identified as a factor in penalty-shot decisions. The argument is not just about technique, but about how fear of embarrassment can push people away from risks worth taking. Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo are both said to have missed penalty kicks in this World Cup. Their inclusion shows that this pressure is not limited to unknown players or marginal moments. Asamoah Gyan’s penalty in the 2010 World Cup quarterfinals is used as an example of pressure affecting composure. The example fits the article’s larger concern with how a decisive kick can become a test of nerve as much as skill. The broader lesson is that fear of embarrassment can keep people from taking worthwhile risks. By linking soccer penalties with decision-making lessons from poker, the article frames risk as something to judge by value, not by how painful failure might look. The Tottenham Hotspurs motto appears at the end as a compact call for courage: "To dare is to do." In the context of the piece, that line reinforces intelligent risk-taking and the need to resist choices driven mainly by ego bias.

original: I don’t think that anyone can claim that evangelicals today have true political power. As The Atlantic said back in July, evangelicals don’t have much to show for their betrayal of Christ as they steadfastly hold onto Trump. They took a gamble and they lost, or to be fair, they won a cruel prize of chaos. Regardless of anything they say, is anybody truly happy in 2020? Do everyday people feel a happiness or peace about politics, the economy, racism, policing, or COVID-19? To say there is a great deal of unrest is, of course, an understatement. But it’s not just the Left that’s been left unhappy. Evangelicals are unhappy too. They think they’re fighting in some holy war against evils like socialism. They turn on Netflix and fear they’re losing a cultural war. Trump’s poor leadership has impacted us all. Further divided us. I daresay it’s even served as the devastatingly perfect experiment for some of the issues discussed in the recent docudrama, The Social Dilemma. Director Jeff Orlowski says the internet is undermining democracy, and that lies spread six times faster online than truth. As it turns out, Trump’s presidency and evangelicalism’s blind spots have converged at this frighteningly ideal point with social media where the facts no longer matter because everybody’s perception of the facts have been clouded by what they want those facts to mean. I wish like hell that I could tell you the solution here is easy, but it’s not. There’s a saying that “You can’t fix stupid but you can vote it out.” Even that is too simplistic, though. Americans are wrestling with mental illness, social media influence, and frankly, stupidity, in a way we’ve never done before. Problems in the world are nothing new. Racism, inequality, and all sorts of political unrest are not issues exclusive to 2020. We shouldn’t be surprised by struggles and unrest, but we should recognize no generation gets through life unscathed. And when we think about American history, not to mention world history, we need to remind ourselves that we are in it. We are making history every damn day. Our actions and errors have consequences with the power to reverberate for generations. It reminds me of the Billy Joel song, “We Didn’t Start the Fire.” After all, we didn’t start the fire. So much of what is happening right now was put into motion long before any of us were old enough to make our own choices. Like me, some of you were raised in an evangelical bubble that stunted your cognitive growth. Maybe it made you more gullible or even “stupid” about certain things. Ironically, there’s no shame (or sin) in being stupid. It’s very human and natural to take the path of least resistance and believe what we’ve been taught when we were very young. And in addition to stunting critical thinking, evangelicalism has had a hand in teaching folks to respond, well, positively to authoritarian parenting and leadership. Of course, authoritarian parenting isn’t limited to evangelicals, but it’s quite common among them and Christians in general. As research professor Peter Gray, Ph.D. writes: “People with an authoritarian mindset believe, first and foremost, in obedience to authority. So, of course, obedience is high on their list of ideal traits for a child; but obedience is also high on their list of ideal traits for people in general. Leaders, especially strong, confident leaders, are to be followed. Authoritarians also tend toward simplistic ways of thinking; things are black or white, right or wrong. If something is right for one person, it should be right for everyone and everyone should see it as right. They don’t tolerate ambiguity and have little taste for subtlety or dissenting opinions. To an authoritarian, the way to solve problems is to find a powerful, confident leader—a sort of superhero who claims in unambiguous language that he can solve your problems—and then follow that person.” I see this weird sort of lust for authoritarian rule a lot, lately. Arguments supporting Trump aren’t debates at all. They’re generally just screaming matches to “get with the program.” For the Trump-supporting, authoritarian-loving person, the President’s critics are just grasping at straws to bring up taxes. They paint any reasonable and valid criticism against Trump as biased or “fake news,” because those are the only options when you lack appropriate critical thinking skills. While it’s no one’s fault to be raised this way, it is up to each individual to not remain stunted in their ability to think critically. Furthermore, we have a responsibility to ensure that younger generations are equipped with the tools they need to think for themselves and acquire the critical thinking skills they will need to make this world a healthier place. This is a big ask. This is going to take work.
sampled: Chinese dissident and artist Ai Weiwei staged a silent protest outside the Old Bailey Court in London during Julian Assange's extradition hearing, drawing attention to a legal proceeding that much of the mainstream press had largely ignored. Standing outside the court, Ai Weiwei spoke plainly about what he believed was at stake, saying of Assange, "He truly represents a core value of why we are free — because we have freedom of the press." Assange's trial was in its fourth week of witness testimony at the time, with the proceedings centered on whether the WikiLeaks founder should be extradited to the United States to face criminal prosecution. U.S. prosecutors had indicted Assange on 17 espionage charges and one charge of computer misuse, all stemming from WikiLeaks' 2010 publication of secret American military documents. The scale of the legal jeopardy Assange faces is difficult to overstate, as the charges carry a maximum sentence of 175 years in prison. That figure alone sets this case apart from nearly any other press freedom prosecution in recent American legal history, and it has drawn condemnation from journalists and civil liberties advocates around the world. Ai Weiwei did not limit himself to the symbolic gesture of his silent vigil, and he spoke directly about the human dimension of Assange's situation. "He is prepared to fight," Ai Weiwei said, "but this is not fair to him. Free him, let him be a free man." Pentagon Papers whistleblower Daniel Ellsberg testified in Assange's defense and directly challenged the U.S. government's core argument that publishing the documents had endangered lives. Ellsberg's testimony carried particular weight given his own history of leaking classified government material and the legal battles he faced in the aftermath. Ellsberg also noted that Assange had withheld 15,000 files from the release of the Afghanistan War Logs, a detail that undermined the prosecution's portrait of Assange as reckless with sensitive information. That decision to hold back tens of thousands of documents suggested a deliberate editorial process rather than an indiscriminate data dump. Assange had requested help from the State Department and the Defense Department to redact names before releasing the documents, but both agencies refused to assist him. That refusal is a significant detail in the defense's argument, since it places responsibility for any potential harm on the government agencies that declined to participate in minimizing risk. No single person has been identified by the U.S. government as having died, been physically harmed, or incarcerated as a direct result of WikiLeaks publications. Rebecca Vincent, director of International Campaigns for Reporters Without Borders reported separately that medical experts had expressed serious concern that Assange could attempt to take his own life while held in detention. The political landscape surrounding Assange has been notable for the bipartisan nature of the hostility directed at him. In 2010, Joe Biden, then a prominent Democratic figure and later the party's presidential nominee, reportedly compared Assange to "a high-tech terrorist," while Donald Trump's administration pursued the prosecution that produced the current indictment. Video journalist Matt Orfalea observed that the Trump administration issued what he described as the first indictment in history charging a publisher for publishing government secrets. That framing cuts to the heart of the press freedom argument, since the charges against Assange do not hinge on hacking or theft but on the act of receiving and publishing classified material. Jonathan Cook, a U.K.-based reporter and press freedom commentator and Alan MacLeod, a columnist for FAIR were among those who drew attention to the uneven media landscape surrounding the case. Critics noted a stark contrast between the extensive mainstream media coverage devoted to Bob Woodward's book published around the same period and the minimal coverage given to Assange's trial. Chelsea Manning, the U.S. soldier who passed the documents to WikiLeaks had already served time in military detention before receiving a commutation, yet the source of the leak received far more public sympathy than the publisher who made the material available to the world. Kevin Gosztola of ShadowProof was among the few journalists providing sustained, detailed coverage of the trial proceedings from inside and outside the court. The gap between the legal stakes of the Assange case and the volume of press attention it received became a recurring point of criticism among those who argued that journalists should have a professional interest in its outcome. A conviction under the Espionage Act on charges rooted in publishing activity would set a precedent that could reach far beyond WikiLeaks and Assange himself. Ai Weiwei's presence outside the Old Bailey Court placed the case in a global context, linking it to broader struggles over state power and the rights of those who expose government conduct. His protest was quiet but pointed and his words connected Assange's individual legal fight to the larger question of whether press freedom retains any practical meaning when a publisher faces 175 years in prison for publishing documents the public had a clear interest in reading.

original: Artificial Intelligence has been re-shaping the world as we know it. Not in the way that we saw in the famous movie the Terminator (SkyNet is not going to take over your phone) but it has transformed our everyday lives by improving processes that we perform regularly. The same holds true for the shipping industry. AI has enabled the implementation of IoT devices that gather information that the AI can learn from, improve upon, and make automated decisions. Automation may be the biggest and most beneficial way AI is used in shipping because it enables anomaly detection, reduction in waste, improved quality control, and decreased shipping times. The combination of IoT devices and AI has brought unparalleled improvements to quality control, fuel consumption, and safety. One example of how AI is aiding the shipping industry is how it improves quality control. With the installation of cameras and IoT devices in cargo containers shipping companies can monitor the environment of goods to prevent damage and spoiling. This is very prevalent in the food transport industry. AI monitors data received from cameras and IoT devices about data points such as temperature, humidity, shock(fall), light exposure, and even vibration. This provides a richer bank of information on the quality of goods not only at the beginning and end of transport but during. Through automated alerts and solution suggestions shipping companies can adjust containers to remedy problems in real-time and prevent the waste or degradation of goods. Artificial Intelligence is also allowing shipping companies to manage their fuel consumption and utilize the most efficient shipping routes. The accurate monitoring of how fuel is being used leads to a reduction in fuel spend and brings environmental benefits by decreasing emissions. AI is also being used to improve the physical routes that shipping companies take. Based on historical data on weather patterns like water and wind currents, traffic through certain areas and ports; shipping companies can plan routes that leverage all of this information to reduce fuel consumption and reduce trip times. Lastly, AI can be used to improve safety by monitoring ship systems and the environment around the ship. An example is a ship image recognition system being developed by tech company SenseTime and Japanese shipping firm Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL). They are developing an image recognition system to identify ships in the surrounding area and monitor shipping lanes. This makes transport within bays, from entering to departing ports, much safer, not only for your ship but the surrounding ships as well. The advent of cheaper and faster computing power, combined with the improvements in the accuracy and efficiency of AI models has brought about a lot of improvements to the shipping industry. Reduction in waste, efficient fuel consumption, and improved safety features are just a few of the ways the shipping industry is becoming faster, safer, and more efficient in the present and future.
sampled: Jon Brosio grew up on the outside of the popular social circles that defined high school for so many people. His friend group was small, his social standing was quiet, and the kind of belonging that seemed effortless for others felt distant to him during those years. That experience shaped how he saw himself and what he believed was possible. After high school, rather than staying close to the familiar, he moved away from home and began building something of his own choosing. The path he took was not guided by a prestigious degree or a set of rare skills that most people lack. What followed was a gradual, deliberate effort to construct a life and a livelihood on terms he set for himself and that process eventually led him to write about it publicly in The Ascent on October 17, 2020. Brosio now earns a healthy living doing work he genuinely enjoys, which is a combination that many people treat as a distant aspiration rather than a practical goal. He also spends part of his time helping others build similar lifestyles, working with people who want to move away from work that feels like a poor fit for who they are. One pattern he noticed when looking back at his graduating class stuck with him that many of the unconventional or quiet peers from those years are now living what he would describe as successful lives. He is careful to acknowledge that this observation carries his own confirmation bias and is not a clean or universal generalization that applies to everyone. Still, the pattern felt meaningful enough to name and it shaped the framing of what he wanted to share. The article he published lays out the strategy he followed to build, scale, and grow an online business, offered to the millions of people who like him have no special skills or particular educational background behind their results. Brosio is direct about the fact that no unusual talent or credential explains where he ended up. He did not arrive at a comfortable, self-directed livelihood because of advantages that most people simply do not have access to. What he describes instead is a strategy that a repeatable set of decisions and actions that he followed over time and that produced real results. The absence of special skills is not a footnote in his account but a central part of the argument he is making to the reader. The strategy he promises to share covers building an online business from early stages through growth and scale. He positions this not as abstract advice but as the specific approach he personally used. His background of being outside the popular group and later moving away from home to forge his own path gives that account a grounded texture. The promise of the article is practical: here is what was done, and here is how it worked.

original: I used to do the same exact thing at the gym, every single week — for years. The same exercises, for the same number of sets. I would simply try to beat the amount of weight I did the week prior, which I would recall by memory. I absolutely didn’t bother to write anything down. Technically, this is a form of progressive overload, and when you’re still a beginner, you can get away with that for a while. Because when you go from doing nothing at all to just about anything, progress will likely be made. But you can only do that for so long before you become stagnant, or worse, get hurt. Once I began implementing proper workout programs, as opposed to just “winging it”, I was able to take my strength & conditioning to the next level. But if I had to do it all over again, I realize now that I could’ve made a lot more progress in a lot less time — if I had followed a properly structured program from the beginning. But no single program is “one size fits all”, and it’s important to know exactly what you’re getting into before you begin one. Consider the following three things before selecting the program that’s right for you. #1 — Assess your fitness level There are many different programs available with varying degrees of difficulty, and the program that you want to do may not be the program that you should do. At least, not at first. The core of every fundamentally sound workout program should be anchored around a few basic movement patterns: a push, a pull, a squat, a hinge, and a lunge. If you’re new to the gym and are unable to properly perform these movements with your bodyweight alone, you shouldn’t jump straight into a program that calls for heavy deadlifts, bench presses, and squats. Rather, opt for a program that teaches you to properly execute these movements in their most basic form — exercises like bodyweight squats and push ups. Once you’ve developed mastery of those movements, then you can gradually progress towards loading those exercises up with additional weight. A progression from a bodyweight push up to a barbell bench press may look something like this: Push ups on an incline bench (note: If you can’t do a pushup, try these instead of doing push ups on your knees. It’s a more natural movement.) (note: If you can’t do a pushup, try these instead of doing push ups on your knees. It’s a more natural movement.) Bodyweight push ups Dumbbell floor press Dumbbell bench press Barbell bench press This progression could be made over the course of several months or even years. It is entirely dependent upon the individual, and how quickly or slowly you progress isn’t important; what is important is that you’re able to “walk before you run”. #2 — Be sure your program aligns with your goals Before beginning a program, have a clear understanding of what and who the program was designed for versus what your specific goals are. If your main goal is to compete on a bodybuilding stage, then a program designed for Olympic weightlifters may not be ideal. I had a friend whose number one goal was to add 50 pounds to his one rep max on the barbell back squat. He purchased the program, ran it for 12 weeks, and was sorely disappointed to find that he was barely squatting 10 pounds more than his previous max by the end of the training cycle. What he didn’t read, which was clearly stated in the program’s description, was that this particular program was designed by somebody with chronic lower back issues, specifically for people who need a way to train their legs without incorporating any heavy barbell work — exactly what my friend was trying to improve. Always have a clear understanding of exactly what you’re doing before you invest the time and the money into doing it. #3 — Autoregulate your training Think of any program you’re on as “written in pencil, not in pen”.
sampled: When a letter from AARP arrived in the mailbox addressed directly to her, Angelica Mordant felt a sharp and sudden reckoning settle over her ordinary afternoon. Her first thought, stated plainly and without ceremony, was "This is it. I'm here. I'm officially old." Mordant was 53 years old at the time, a number she had carried without much ceremony until that envelope made it feel suddenly official and impossible to ignore. The AARP letter did what calendars and mirrors had not quite managed: it turned an abstract awareness of aging into something concrete sitting in her hands. Her first instinct was to call her sister, the person most likely to understand the specific mix of humor and genuine unease that the letter had stirred up inside her. Her sister is 15 years older than Mordant which meant she had already passed through this particular doorway and come out the other side with perspective to spare. When Mordant told her sister about the AARP letter, the sister's response reframed the situation immediately and with characteristic sharpness. "You think that's bad? I get mail from crematoriums and funeral homes!" she said, which managed to be both funny and oddly clarifying at the same time. The laughter faded into something more earnest when the sister shifted from jokes to genuine counsel, offering words that Mordant clearly took seriously. "Sissy, make your memories NOW. You're wondering where 30 years went? You have 10-15 good years left before you really start slowing down. Enjoy the time you have left. Make these years count." That advice landed differently than the AARP letter had because it came from someone who had lived the years Mordant was only beginning to reckon with and who spoke from direct experience rather than institutional assumption. The sister's framing of 10 to 15 good years was not meant as a warning so much as an instruction to stop deferring the life she had been quietly postponing. Mordant had been deferring quite a lot, including a long-held dream of owning a pink vintage camper and taking road trips she had been putting off for 30 years. That specific image, the pink camper and the open road, represents the kind of concrete desire that tends to get buried under the practical weight of ordinary life until something like an AARP letter shakes it loose again. She was also honest about the physical realities of being in her 50s, noting changes that included wrinkles, reduced strength, and a shoulder injury she sustained from the simple act of starting a lawnmower. These details are not complaints so much as an acknowledgment that the body keeps its own honest record of time passing, separate from how a person might feel on the inside. On the domestic side of aging, Mordant noted that hosting large family holiday dinners had been passed on to her children, a shift that carries its own quiet significance. Handing over that particular responsibility marks a change in generational role that no letter from any organization could have announced quite so clearly. Rather than letting the AARP letter close the conversation about aging on a deflating note, Mordant responded by compiling a list of 12 reasons why being over 50 carries genuine advantages worth naming. That act of list-making was itself a kind of argument, a deliberate choice to look at the same set of facts and find the case for appreciation rather than dread. She also announced plans to join the Red Hat Society, a social group whose existence is essentially a collective declaration that women past a certain age intend to take up space and enjoy themselves without apology. That plan placed alongside the pink camper dream suggests someone who is taking her sister's advice seriously and translating it into actual intentions rather than vague aspirations. The piece was published on March 7, 2020, at a moment when Mordant's personal reckoning with time had just been catalyzed by a single piece of unsolicited mail. What the AARP letter actually delivered was not a reminder of limitation but a prompt to stop wondering where 30 years went and start being deliberate about the years still ahead.

original: Therapists Face Different Challenges with Telehealth ”In a moment, saving a bird” Photo by Pierre Bamin on Unsplash The pandemic has forced medical professionals including mental health professionals to rethink how they do their jobs. I called my client promptly at 10 am for an appointment we had scheduled. No answer. I called a few more times. About 10:10, I got this text. ”In a minute, saving a bird.” Ok, then. I like birds. I wonder what kind of bird? I pictured her putting it back in a nest or in a box in a warm place, or? I waited til about 10:30 then got another text “do you have time later today? Well of course I have time but…. Isn’t it my time? Already designated for relaxing with my husband. Or taking a walk or starting dinner? Or just being quiet and alone? Boundaries get blurred The pandemic has forced medical professionals including mental health professionals to rethink how they do their jobs. Since early March, after a scare with a client who had been exposed to the virus, I have been doing therapy from home. Of course, this is safer for me and my family. I am in my 70s and live with a man in his 70s who has several risk factors as well. The thought of sitting in a small room across from people who may not be as careful as I am, talking and gesturing and laughing and crying, (and how do you do therapy with a mask, for Pete’s sake?) sounded like a set up for catching and spreading the virus. I was freaked out in March. I went home, set up an office there, and began using the telephone and internet to connect with my clients. My main goal was to keep talking with my people, to console, encourage, and steady them as we all went through this pandemic for a few months. The few months turned into six with no end in sight. I didn’t want to keep paying rent and utilities for an unused office so decided to give it up. Now I work from home permanently. I set up some office hours but it’s hard to stick to them, because of birds. And other things. So I tell my client, yes, we could talk at 2:30 this afternoon. That’s within my stated office hours. Even though I had hoped to be finished before then, I can deal with it. That’s what I’m here for. Some time before 2:30 she calls to cancel, saying she’s too tired and can we talk tomorrow morning. Tomorrow is Friday, my day off. No, I’m not doing that. My usual policy with people who miss appointments for non-emergency reasons is to have a talk about the value of my time and the need to prioritize their treatment. If this were a client with private insurance I could charge my standard $75 missed appointment fee. This is not possible in this case. So I take the loss of income, because of a bird. But I like birds. Creative excuses When I worked at the mental health practice of the local hospital system, the staff kept a running list of creative excuses clients gave for missing their appointments. Here is a sampling: I missed my appointment because: My dog just had puppies I’m stuck on the rotary and can’t get off I’m expecting my period I might be getting depressed I’m too anxious (the only reasonable one) My kids won’t stop whining To which I could add I’m saving a bird While clients don’t have to drive to see me now, invalidating all the excuses involving flat tires, keys locked in the car, money for gas, and the danger of driving in ice and snow in winter, instead, there are different excuses like this one: I need to get my husband/child breakfast, the internet just went down and Joey has to go online for school, my wife can’t find the car keys, etc. And there are many more interruptions than in my pleasant, private office. I listen to children fighting and ruining their parent’s train of thought; I tolerate cats swishing grandly past the screen, tails high (and close-ups of cat butts). There are the occasional tantrums of younger children, endless arguments with older ones, requests for help from unknowing, and sometimes undressed, spouses. On top of that, there are situations like the long-awaited plumber arriving just as we are about to start. Or a virtual meeting with a doctor rearranged for our appointment time. Of course, if my clients were organized and assertive with good time management skills and clear priorities, meeting with me might be unnecessary. But I know they need help with these things. This is a new age for all of us and most of us are trying our best to stay afloat, help our fellows and figure out creative ways to solve problems.
sampled: Black History Month offers a natural occasion to look closely at African American writers whose work shaped the literary and political landscape of the United States across the twentieth century. Three figures stand out in particular: Margaret Walker, Samuel Alfred Beadle, and Amiri Baraka, each of whom built a body of work that reached well beyond regional or generational limits. Margaret Walker was born in 1915 and died in 1998, leaving behind a legacy that includes a historic first: she became the first black woman to win a national literary prize in America. She was also the first person of color included in the Yale Younger Poets Series, a distinction that announced her talent to the country at large. The Yale Younger Poets Series had been running since 1918 when Walker's collection For My People was selected in 1942 by series editor Stephen Vincent Benét. That selection placed Walker in a tradition of recognized American poetry and gave her work a platform that few black writers of her era had been able to access. Before that recognition, Walker had already been deepening her craft through community and mentorship, joining a Chicago writing group led by Richard Wright. That experience connected her to one of the most serious literary networks of the period and shaped the political awareness that would run through all her later writing. Walker's novel Jubilee appeared in 1966 after nearly three decades of research and drafting, making it one of the most sustained literary projects of its time. The book was translated into seven languages and sold more than a million copies, reaching readers far outside the United States. Jubilee is grounded in the life of Walker's maternal great-grandmother, tracing black experience through slavery, the Civil War, and the years of emancipation. The novel unfolds across fifty-eight chapters, giving the narrative the scope and weight of an epic rooted in personal and historical memory. Walker spent more than twenty years teaching at Jackson State University, where she founded the Institute for the Study of the History, Life, and Culture of Black People. That institution extended her influence beyond the page, creating a scholarly home for research into black history and culture in the South. Samuel Alfred Beadle, who lived from 1857 to 1932, worked as an attorney and storyteller as well as a poet, and his career unfolded in Mississippi during a period when black writers faced severe obstacles to publication and recognition. He was one of only eight black writers in Mississippi whose work gained recognition outside the state in the early twentieth century. Beadle's second poetry collection, Lyrics of the Underworld, appeared in 1912 and carried a distinctive visual element alongside its verse. The volume featured sixteen photographs taken by his son, who went on to become one of Mississippi's best known black photographers, making the book a collaboration across generations and art forms. Amiri Baraka, born Leroy Jones in 1934, built his early reputation in Manhattan's literary world during the late 1950s and early 1960s. He was the only black writer to establish a significant presence in the Beat-inspired literary scene there between 1958 and 1965, navigating a creative environment that was largely white while developing a voice that was distinctly his own. Baraka's play Dutchman won a prestigious Obie Award in 1964, bringing him widespread critical attention and establishing his reputation as a major voice in American theater. The play's confrontational style reflected the tensions of its era and marked Baraka as a writer willing to place race and power at the center of dramatic form. The assassination of Malcolm X proved to be a turning point that radicalized Baraka and redirected the course of his work and public life. He moved away from the predominantly white downtown literary world and toward a more explicitly political engagement with black identity, community, and struggle. Baraka joined the faculty of African Studies at SUNY-Stony Brook in 1980 and taught there for two decades bringing his political and artistic commitments into the academic setting. His major poetry collection Hard Facts stands as one of the key texts from this period of his career, reflecting the ideological seriousness that defined his later writing. Among the honors Baraka received were a PEN-Faulkner Award and the Langston Hughes Medal both in 1989, recognizing the breadth and significance of his contributions to American literature. These awards came during a period when his teaching, writing, and public advocacy were all active and interlocked. Baraka also wrote an appreciation of Margaret Walker among his late works composed after her death in 1998, connecting two of the most consequential African American writers of the twentieth century through his tribute. That gesture acknowledged Walker's foundational role in a tradition that Baraka himself had done so much to extend and challenge. Taken together, the careers of Walker, Beadle, and Baraka trace a long arc of African American literary achievement that moved through poetry, fiction, drama, and scholarship. Each writer worked under different pressures and toward different ends, but all three built work that documented, challenged, and enriched the world they inhabited.

original: Do you know about the Law of Unintended Consequences? It broadly comes down to this: Any action that involves a complex system is certain to have unintended consequences. This is especially relevant in the field of machine learning where we are working with highly complex software. Machine learning systems almost always have unintended side-effects. Here’s a beautiful example. Consider a Deep Convolutional Inverse Graphics Network, or DCIGN. It looks like this: It may look complicated, but a DCIGN is actually made up of a convolutional neural network (CNN) and a deconvolutional Network (DN), mounted end-to-end. The first half reads in an image and converts it to abstract information called a ‘feature map’. The green nodes in the middle can then make subtle changes to the map, and the second half takes the modified map and reconstructs it back into an image. So in a nutshell a DCIGN reads in an image, makes changes, and produces a new image. The most famous DCIGN is CycleGAN, which can do mind-blowing stuff like this: Look at the Monet –> photo conversion. A hundred years ago, Claude Monet saw that river scene and turned it into a painting. CycleGAN just ran that process in reverse, and reconstructed a photorealistic image from his painting. Isn’t that mind-blowing? It seems as if you can do anything with CycleGAN. So researchers at Google and Stanford asked themselves if you could use CycleGAN to map satellite photos to street maps and back again. The results exceeded their wildest expectations. Look at this: A perfect mapping from an aerial photo to a street map and back again. Amazing, right? But look closer. Look at that white building at the bottom of the image. See all those skylights on the roof? They’re not in the middle image! And yet, they reappear in the final image. So how did the second half of the DCIGN network know where to put them all back? Common sense tells us that this is impossible. And our common sense is correct. The AI actually cheated! The researchers gave the software an impossible task, and it found a loophole and cheated. Let’s start with the basics. We know that mapping aerial photos to street maps and back again is impossible, because we lose information when we convert the photo to a street map. Subtle details like the position of skylights and smokestacks on roofs are lost. And yet, the software managed to reconstruct a perfect aerial photo. So it somehow managed to hide all these details in the middle image without us noticing. Let’s take a closer look at the middle image. We’re going to crank up the contrast to reveal small color differences: Do you see that? There’s actually a wealth of information hidden in the map image, encoded as tiny color changes that are imperceptible to human eyes. You can see lots of red pixels clustered around the white building. These are used by the second half of the DCIGN to draw the skylights in the correct place on the roof. This is the equivalent of the AI cheating and secretly writing down all the test answers to pass an exam To test their theory, the researches played a trick on the AI. They used a different map image, but overlaid it with the ‘cheat notes’ from the original map. If the AI really is cheating, it’s going to ignore the new map and reconstruct the original aerial photo from the cheat notes. And here are the results: And that proves it. The software is only using the cheat data to reconstruct the aerial photo, it’s completely ignoring the street map. So here’s the moral of this story: Be very careful when you are building machine learning solutions, because computers will always try to give you the result you ask for. If you give them an impossible task, they will simply find a loophole and cheat. If the results of your AI app seem too good to be true, they probably are. So always make sure to include a test that catches your software off guard to expose any cheating. How do you feel about AI’s cheating? Do you think it’s funny, cute, or scary? Add a comment and let me know!
sampled: John Ridley Stroop was born in 1897 as the second youngest of six children and spent his early years on a family farm in Tennessee, a rural upbringing that gave little indication of the psychological legacy he would leave behind. He went on to study experimental psychology and education, graduating at the top of his class and demonstrating the kind of academic discipline that would shape his later research. Stroop's most enduring contribution is a deceptively simple test that measures a person's ability to name the ink colour of a word that spells a different colour name and the results consistently show that this incongruence slows response times in measurable ways. The test captures something fundamental about how the human brain handles competing streams of information, forcing the mind to suppress one well-learned process in order to complete another. When people are asked to read the word itself while ignoring the ink colour, the interference largely disappears which suggests that reading words is a more automatic process than identifying colours from visual input. This asymmetry points to a hierarchy in perceptual processing, where some cognitive tasks run more fluently than others and therefore resist disruption more effectively. Stroop's research did not emerge in isolation but built on earlier work initiated by Wilhelm Wundt, who directed his student James Cattell to investigate the relationship between colour naming and colour-word reading in controlled conditions. That lineage of inquiry gave Stroop a foundation to work from, and his own experiments refined and formalized the interference phenomenon in ways that earlier researchers had not fully articulated. The effect Stroop documented is not limited to colour words and coloured ink. It extends to direction words displayed in incongruent locations or orientations on a screen, showing that the underlying mechanism of cognitive interference operates across different categories of meaning and spatial perception. Research has also examined incongruence involving numbers, and one study found that numerical stimuli differing in both their numerical value and their physical size on screen caused participants to identify them more slowly than congruent versions. The interference pattern holds even when the competing dimensions are entirely abstract, which points to how broadly the brain applies meaning-based processing during perception. Emotional words introduce a related but distinct layer of complexity into the classic Stroop task, slowing colour naming in ways that neutral words do not and they are also recalled more easily when participants face unexpected memory tests afterward. This dual effect suggests that emotional content captures attention during processing and leaves a more durable trace in memory than neutral material does. A study examining faces of men, women, and houses paired with either congruent or incongruent labels found that participants remembered the incongruent pairings better than the congruent ones. That finding aligns with the broader pattern in which mismatched information demands more from the perceptual system and, in doing so, becomes more firmly encoded. The explanation for why incongruent stimuli are better remembered has been described directly by researchers: "Transient shifts of attention in response to perceptual processing difficulty … appear to strengthen the encoding of incongruent items as they are processed." That account frames the memory advantage not as a quirk but as a predictable consequence of the extra cognitive work that incongruence requires. Colin MacLeod identified what he saw as the twin sources of Stroop's lasting influence: "Its large and always statistically reliable effect and the lack of an adequate explanation for the effect." That combination of empirical robustness and theoretical openness has kept researchers returning to the phenomenon across decades, applying it to new domains and stimuli. Outside the laboratory, Stroop spent most of his career teaching at David Lipscomb College and preached each Sunday, living a life that ran parallel tracks between academic work and religious commitment. The contours of that career reveal a person whose interests extended well beyond the single experiment that made his name recognisable in psychology. By the end of his life, Stroop had published 7 biblical books compared to just 4 psychology papers, a ratio that reflects how much of his intellectual energy went into theological writing rather than experimental science.

original: Image by Kevinsphotos from Pixabay Telling a lie is forgivable, but living a lie is not. By constructing your world from lies, only destruction will come. Even the smallest lie, if left unacknowledged, can kill any form of love. Occasionally, I’ll ask people if they’re honest. Are you a liar? I’ll say. Pointless question, right? The dishonest would just lie about it. More revealing is how people think about their own lies — the specifications they give. How often? When? The details mean more. The reasons are way more interesting. The most dangerous liars aren’t the ones who lie all the time. The real shits are the ones who lie all the time AND claim to be terrible liars. Oh, I suck at lying. I’m incapable of telling anything but the truth. Be wary of anyone who says this. They’re the same people who say they don’t understand the point of telling a lie—that such a reprehensible quality is simply beyond them. Everyone knows the point of lying — it’s to distort reality. The real honest people — the truth seekers, the ones with integrity, the people who are self-aware — these people usually admit to it when it matters most. When the stakes are high, when the cost involves hurting another — when the effects actually mean something, the honest people come clean. They don’t double down. They want to purge themselves of this awful tendency. They would feel appalled by how much they’ve lied, dismayed to the point of guilt and disappointment. So, ultimately, I don’t fear the casual liar, because I am one. All writers are. It’s a very human thing. It’s a very real thing. Anyone who uses language can frame something in such a way that it no longer resembles the truth. The people I really fear are the ones who have so thoroughly convinced themselves of their own honesty that they lose all ability to even recognize the most obvious deceit within themselves. It is the self-deceiver who is most disconnected from reality and causes the most damage and pain to others.
sampled: One of the most practical principles in software development is limiting the scope of variables and references as much as possible, a discipline that Nick Hodges examines in detail in his article published in Better Programming. When a variable's scope is kept narrow, the number of places in a codebase where that variable can be modified shrinks considerably making the code far easier to reason about and trace when something goes wrong. Global variables sit at the opposite end of this spectrum, and they are widely considered harmful precisely because there is no reliable way to know where or when they might be changed across a large program. Object-oriented programming addresses this problem directly through encapsulation, which formalizes the process of limiting scope by bundling data with the methods that are permitted to act on it. Information hiding takes this idea a step further by restricting variable scope so that values cannot be changed except through explicitly allowed pathways, giving developers a controlled and predictable interface rather than an open field of potential modifications. This kind of discipline also reduces the ability for code to create unwanted dependencies between classes which is a quieter but equally important benefit of keeping scope tight. Loose coupling, the deliberate limiting of dependencies within a system, is considered a sound practice because it keeps individual components independent enough to be understood and modified in isolation. Tight coupling produces the opposite effect, making code hard to test and difficult to maintain as the system grows and requirements shift over time. A related hazard is what developers call action at a distance, the situation where a change made in one area of a codebase produces unintended side effects in a completely separate area often in ways that are difficult to diagnose. Hodges points to declaring const whenever possible as a subtle but effective language-level technique for limiting scope, since it signals intent clearly and prevents accidental reassignment.

original: Improve Your Future By Looking To The Past: I could spout on and on about why reducing your carbon footprint will benefit you. But I’ll keep my reasoning simple: Anytime you can apply an understanding of human evolution to your present-day life, you will be better off. We evolved to live in harmony with nature. We evolved to mostly eat lower on the food chain — think fruits and vegetables, not factory-bred meat and sugar-laden processed foods. We evolved to be on our feet, not on a comfortable couch or an ergonomic desk chair. We evolved to spend time outside. We evolved to derive pleasure from the simple things in life — socializing with friends and loved ones, not scrolling on a screen to find edited pictures to like or things to buy that you don’t need and are probably ecologically harmful. We evolved to live life in the slow lane, not the fast lane. We evolved to live surrounded by plants and rocks, not concrete and asphalt. Your ancestors lived very sustainable lifestyles. It was good for them, their neighbors, and the finite planet they lived on. The more you can emulate your ancestors in this respect, the better off you’ll be. Maybe that goes against the gospel of progress and futurism, but I’m a bit skeptical that many of the technological advancements we’ve made lately as a civilization — cars, TVs, smartphones, etc — have truly heightened our sense of well-being. Call me crazy, but sometimes I wish I could enter a time machine and go back 10,000 or 20,000 years. Sure, Stone Age people had hard, risky lives back in the day. They toiled to find clean food and water. They faced harsh conditions and were always vulnerable to violence and predation. Trouble awaited them with every step and every breath. Nonetheless, I don’t think they were significantly worse off than we are today. They didn’t pollute their air and poison their water with deadly chemicals. They didn’t stare at screens all day and play dangerous fake comparison games with each other. They didn’t ‘buy’ things they didn’t need. They didn’t eat processed crap. They didn’t lounge around and sit on their asses. They didn’t build concrete cages divorced from nature. They lived life to the fullest. And so can you. You can choose to adopt many of their wise practices, but you can benefit from the cars, antibiotics, supermarkets, and smartphones we take for granted. You can choose to embrace the aspects of modern life that are good for you and embrace the aspects of ancient life that are good for you. You have the best deck of cards any generation has ever had. If you play your hand correctly, you can live a better life than anyone ever has. And your lifestyle will become a smaller slice of the carbon footprint pie. Spend some time thinking deeply about what aspects of modern life truly benefit you. Then, think about what the ancients did that you too can do to cultivate your well-being. Take advantage of the pandemic to reconnect with nature and thereby reconnect with yourself. You may never have a better opportunity to bridge the gap between your authentic self and the inauthentic aspects of your self you present to the world.
sampled: Consumer choice alone will not solve the climate crisis. A UNEP report makes clear that past sustainable transitions were not driven by people voluntarily deciding to consume more responsibly. Social norms and changing product availability have been the main causes of substantial behavioral change. The richest 1% are identified as the primary target group for the lifestyle changes needed to meaningfully reduce greenhouse gas emissions across the global economy. Urban planning in the developed world has long catered to a car-dominant society, shaped largely by the accessibility wealthy individuals have always had to private vehicles. It is not uncommon for a wealthy household to own two vehicles and that pattern of ownership has quietly dictated how cities are built and how infrastructure budgets are spent. Roads expand, parking lots multiply, and public transit is treated as secondary. Reducing transportation emissions requires urban planning that deliberately emphasizes walkable and bikeable cities rather than continuing to optimize for the car. That shift demands political will not just consumer preference because the built environment does not change simply because a handful of individuals decide to walk more. Governments and planners must redesign the physical landscape to make low-emission choices the default. The infrastructure itself has to change before behavior reliably follows. Social influence acts as a real catalyst for lifestyle change through peer pressure and the gradual challenging of societal norms. That same mechanism has historically worked against green initiatives by making wealthy lifestyles appear desirable and worth emulating. Disrupting habitual behavior is described as necessary to break down the barriers that keep people locked into unsustainable routines. Incentives, targeted information and expanded choice have all been deployed to nudge people toward sustainable lifestyles, but the UNEP report is candid that these tools are rarely sufficient for the kind of profound change the climate situation demands. Achieving the objectives of the Paris Agreement requires deep-rooted socioeconomic, cultural, political, and behavioral changes that involve both wealthy individuals and the governments that set the rules around them. Infrastructure improvements such as electric vehicle charging ports and efficient public transport networks are necessary to support sustainable lifestyles at scale. Integrated policies that combine structural, social, contextual, and personal approaches are proposed as the framework for encouraging change among the wealthiest. Social norms shift when the environment around people shifts first. That combination of policy and infrastructure is what the UNEP report points toward as the realistic path forward. Neither goodwill nor individual guilt is a sufficient engine for the scale of change required. Personal virtue matters far less than structural context. The UNEP report is explicit that social norms and product availability have historically driven the most significant and lasting behavioral shifts in society. Achieving Paris Agreement objectives requires changes that run far deeper than shopping habits, cultural values, political systems, and the everyday behavioral patterns of the world's wealthiest people. Wealthy individuals shape demand signals that ripple through entire economies and the lifestyles they normalize tend to set aspirational benchmarks for everyone else. Governments cannot treat this dynamic as a background condition and expect voluntary nudges to compensate for it. Integrated policies that address social, contextual, and personal dimensions simultaneously offer a more credible path than any single-lever approach.

original: Streamlit Streamlit Demo — Source Do you want to create dashboards quickly in Python?. — Streamlit is your best option. Streamlit revolutionises creating web applications with easy to use API and constant feature development. It was only last year October when this open-source tool was launched and no doubt its popularity has increased rapidly in the data science community. Today, Streamlit boosts more functionalities with its recent introduction of streamlit component, where the developer community adds new functionalities. What I like about streamlit is that it has the shortest learning curve of all Python Dashboard creating tools in this list. It offers simple API with excellent documentation and lets you develop applications with less code in pure python. In simple terms, Streamlit empowers you to focus on what matters rather than thinking about front-end back-end technology stacks to use for your project. Panel Panel Gapminder Demo — Source Do you want to create powerful and advanced dashboards in Pure Python with declarative and reactive programming? — Panel is your best bet. Panel is an open-source Python library that lets you create custom interactive web apps and dashboards by connecting user-defined widgets to plots, images, tables, or text. While it is possible to work Streamlit in Jupyter notebooks, we use primarily with Python files. If your favourite data science tool is Jupyter Notebook, then Panel offers extensive support for all plotting libraries. The learning curve is steeper than Streamlit. However, it is simple to create an interactive web application in Panel, using less code with widgets and parameters. Deploying and sharing your web applications and dashboards in Panel is easy. You can display your dashboards inside Jupyter Notebooks, render it as Ipywidgets, run it from the command line, or deploy it using popular tools like Heroku, MyBinder or even other cloud platforms. Voilà Voilà Demo — Source. Do you want to turn your Jupyter Notebooks quickly into standalone web applications? Voilà is for your service. However, you can create interactive reports with widgets in Jupyter notebook using Ipywidgets. You can also use Viola to render any content on Notebooks into Dashboards. You can make coherent Dashboards with Voilà, but that needs you to format your experiments and code in Jupyter notebooks accordingly or suppress and hide unused code and markdowns. Plotly Dash Plotly Dash Demo — Source Do you need more advanced and production-grade level dashboards in Python? — Plotly Dash covers that. Plotly Dash focuses on production and enterprise dashboard creation but also offers free and open-source options in Python, R and Julia. It is the most mature option on this list. Although Dash empowers users to build and deploy web applications without full-stack and DevOps tools in hours, it has the steepest learning curve of all the options in this article. That is also changing with the introduction of Plotly Express — easy to use and high-level API for creating figures with Plotly Libary. I find the Plotly Express library one of my favourite data visualisation tools in Python. Deploying your Plotly Dashboards in your local environment is easy, and you need to deploy it to a server if you need to share it outside. Final Thoughts The choice of your dashboard tool depends on your project needs. Streamlit is for creating quick and versatile dashboard apps with an easy learning curve and less code. I find Streamlit the easiest and the best tool out there to create data visualisation web apps.
sampled: Most productivity advice feels compelling at first, offering tidy systems and step-by-step frameworks that promise to transform how you work, yet Niklas Göke argues that nearly all of it fails over the long run not because the techniques themselves are broken, but because the entire body of conventional advice rests on false assumptions about human nature. Those assumptions quietly undermine every checklist and time-block schedule before the second week is out, leaving people wondering why the method that worked for someone else refuses to work for them. The deeper problem is that conventional productivity culture ignores how humans actually function at a biological and psychological level and in doing so it neglects the true purpose that productivity is supposed to serve in a person's life. When the foundation is wrong, every technique built on top of it inherits that wrongness and the result is a cycle of enthusiasm followed by exhaustion followed by guilt that repeats itself indefinitely. Human brains are wired to seek problems rather than rest in calm, which means that the moment one difficulty is resolved the mind naturally begins scanning for the next issue to fix and this restless orientation is not a personal flaw but a feature of how cognition is structured. Calm is not the default state that productivity systems tend to assume it is, and any approach that treats a clear to-do list as a finish line misunderstands the biological reality of the person trying to use it. Compounding this problem is the role of dopamine, which rewards the completion of even small goals and creates a pull toward chasing more tasks regardless of whether those tasks serve any meaningful priority. That neurological reinforcement loop explains why people can spend an entire day crossing items off a list and still feel oddly hollow at the end, because the brain's reward system and a person's actual values are not always pointed in the same direction. People also tend to overestimate how much they can accomplish within a given stretch of time and underestimate how long individual tasks will take, a well-documented pattern that Göke attributes to the planning fallacy, and this bias is baked so deeply into how people plan their days that it operates largely below conscious awareness. The result is a perpetual gap between the day that was imagined on Sunday evening and the day that actually unfolds on Monday, and most productivity frameworks offer no honest accounting for that gap. Göke redefines productivity in a way that absorbs this reality rather than fighting it, describing it as making good-enough progress on what one cares about most amid the unavoidable chaos of life, which shifts the measure of success away from volume of output and toward alignment with genuine priorities. Paired with this redefinition is his argument that managing expectations of time matters more than managing time itself, because a person who holds realistic expectations can adapt when things go sideways rather than treating every disruption as a personal failure. The practical shape of this approach involves building a system optimized for minimum stress rather than maximum effort, one that includes buffers and deliberate room to fail so that the inevitable interruptions of ordinary life do not collapse the entire structure. Accepting that life involves chance, coincidence, and luck is presented not as defeatism but as a prerequisite for seeing productivity with a genuinely new purpose, because a system that cannot bend will eventually break the person relying on it. Göke locates the site of true productivity not in external outputs or completed task lists but in the mind itself arguing that the internal state a person maintains while working is the actual substance of what productivity means. A stress minimizing approach, produces greater happiness, less burnout, and more calm, which are outcomes that the conventional hustle-oriented model rarely names as goals at all, even though they are precisely what most people are hoping to find when they first go looking for a better way to work.

original: Microsoft recently released a New Dialogue Ranking Pretrained Transformers model. Some human replies are more engaging than others, spawning more followup interactions. Since we want our conversational models to be more interactive we need some metric to know which comment is more likely to engage the user. So authors of DialogRPT trained it on 133M pairs of human feedback data to address this issue and the resulting ranker outperformed several baselines. If you are not interested in paper summary directly jump to the code. Why do we need such a pretrained transformer model? Human-like conversations are perhaps one of the most difficult challenges of AI. Now with more recent advancements in the field some times human annotators cannot reliably distinguish between human- and machine-generated responses. However human responses are not limited to be just relevant to the context. Sometimes they are interesting enough to prompt a rich listener reaction. (Although conversation can be sometimes very boring, heated, funny and awkward🤭).On the other side Chatbots or Conv-AI models just to prevent them from creating inappropriate comments often end up being vague, not engaging. GIF via Giphy A successful dialog turn must be proactive, engaging, and consistent with social norms. The solutions that authors proposed is using existing human feedback data (e.g., number of replies and likes) from online social communities(here Reddit). While there has been work on feedback prediction, this is the first time it has been applied to a dialogue and response generation system. Fig 1. Example of an engaging Dialogue. Courtesy: DialogRPT Let's dive deep on how the model solves the issue of engaging comments. Posts and comments typically form a tree structure. Each comment has its own number of replies and upvotes (refer Fig 1. Upvotes also termed as “Likes” in some social communities). These can be used as engagingness labels after careful normalization and formulation. Using a dataset of 133M pairs of human comments and their associated number of replies or up-/downvotes, authors train a set of large-scale transformer-based feedback ranking models which outperform several baselines. Understanding feedback metrics Posts and comments typically form a tree structure. Consider parent node as context c and the reply to it as r. For each dialogue (c, r), we consider the following feedback: Width, the number of direct replies to r; Depth, the maximum length of the dialogue after this turn; and Updown, the number of upvotes minus the number of downvotes. The feedback metrics defined above cannot be directly used as a measure of reply engagingness. Studies show that while popularity, measured by Updown, generally increases with quality, posts of similar quality can exhibit very different upvote counts. Tasks Given a context and a list of responses, the task of predicting a ranking based on the feedback they received, as measured by these three separate metrics: (1) Width, (2) Depth, and (3) Updown. Along with this an additional task (4)human-vs-fake, which measures how human-like the response is. Problem Formulation and Training objective Contrastive learning approach was used while training the model for the task. A Contrastive Learning approach: Given the confounding factors affecting feedback mentioned above, we train the model on pairs of samples (c, r+) and (c, r−), rather than fitting it to score each dialogue individually. The model is trained in such a way that predicts a higher score for a better response than the less appropriate response. Model ensemble For machine generation: The machine generation is required to be both human-like and preferred by a human. To rank the machine generations, the authors took the probability of joint distributions as follows : P(r = preferred, human-like|c) = P(r = preferred|r = human-like, c)· P(r = human-like|c) Human calibration: To estimate the correlation between the feedback score and human responses preferences, pair of responses for the same context to a set of human annotators, asking them to select the response they would prefer to send or receive. Model and training The model is a 12-layer transformer model based on GPT-2 architecture and initialized with DialoGPTmedium model weights. DialoGPT is a large-scale dialogue response generation model, pre-trained on 147M Reddit conversations. Each model ( for up-down, width, depth, human vs rand) has 354.8M parameters and is trained on an Nvidia Tesla V100 4-core GPU with batch size 256 at an average training speed of 0.33 M pairs of samples per hour. Each model took around 70 hours to converge (until validation loss on a fixed set of 1024 samples ceased to improve). Findings Responses that receive fewer replies or upvotes tend to be less contentful. In contrast, comments that attract more feedback are typically different in character: for instance, questions (indicated by ?, why, how, what, who) often lead to a longer conversation (greater Depth). The model trained only on Width data can perform reasonably well on Depth prediction, and vice versa, consistent with the high correlation between their labels. The Updown label is less correlated with these, and so the model trained on Updown data performs poorly on Width and Depth data. This is in keeping with the complementary relationship between these models.

original: 2. Programmers Shouldn’t Be Insecure About Their Work Now, I’ve got some really skilled senior developers working with me. They are competent individuals who require high standards from my pull requests. Otherwise, they will easily reject them without remorse. I used to think of these people as developers not capable of doing any wrong. I would look at them in awe and wonder if one day I would reach their level of skills and never code anything incorrectly. But this belief was wrong. It didn’t take much for me to gain more experience and dialogue with my colleagues, only to realize that they have insecurities too. They don't always know everything and are not always sure about the best possible solution for a given problem. They have to constantly renew their knowledge like I have to. They know that sometimes they just have to go with the flow and their intuition on what is best for the project. I’ve freed myself from this belief and now I don’t always feel stuck in my own world thinking that I will never be a senior developer because I know that seniors have my feelings of insecurity too.

If someone politely asks you to modify your behaviour and you flat out refuse; that should tell you something. You don’t understand the word “inappropriate”. sampled: Kern Carter wrote a full manuscript in two months which is a pace he had never achieved before. Every previous manuscript had taken him at least a year to complete. The process began in mid-June when an opportunity arrived while he was on vacation in Mexico. He returned home and immediately built a rigorous daily schedule around the project. His mornings started with a writing block from 5:00 am to 8:30 am. Then he shifted to freelance work from 9 to 5 before returning to the manuscript from 7:00 pm to 10:00 pm. Spending 12 to 13 hours each day in front of a laptop became the norm. The push was designed to finish the 60,000 word manuscript in time for a conference at the end of August. When he finally shared the work with agents the feedback landed hard. One agent told him “The concept of the story is good but the writing is not what I expected.” Another agent said “It’s just not all the way thought out.” A third offered the observation “You have something here, but it’s not fully baked.” Carter felt a disappointment as he absorbed the responses. He already knew the work was not his best. The urgency he had imposed on himself created a mental anguish. It also produced a delusion that blinded him to the quality of the writing. He later admitted that ego was the true engine. The drive for acknowledgement had outpaced the actual craft. The experience taught him that the work must come first before any pursuit of success. Seeking validation too early only distorts the creative process. He realized he needs more time and a deeper investment in education to become a better writer. There are no shortcuts that can replace slow growth. He is thankful for the whole experience because it clarified his own writing process. The failure became a necessary mirror.
